Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 46, verse 3:

﴿We did not create the heavens and the earth and what is between them except in truth and for a specified term. But those who disbelieve turn away from what they are warned of.﴾

Since among the most important things the Qur'an brings is establishing the Oneness of God, the Most High, and establishing the Resurrection and recompense — because the benefit of warning depends on establishing these two — His saying ﴿The revelation of the Book is from God, the Mighty, the Wise﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 2] was made a preface to the argument for establishing Oneness, the Resurrection, and recompense. Thus the creation of the heavens and the earth was made a point of agreement, and it was made to follow that this creation was only accompanied by truth. Its being accompanied by truth requires that it not be creation in vain, but rather it indicates that it is followed by a recompense for what created beings do.

The exception "in truth" (bil-haqq) is from general circumstances, meaning: We did not create them except in the state of being accompanied by truth.

His saying ﴿But those who disbelieve turn away from what they are warned of﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relating to the implied pronoun in the prepositional phrase "in truth" (bil-haqq). The purpose of the circumstantial clause is thereby to express wonder at them, and this is not a coordination (ʿatf), because the report about those who disbelieve being turned away is dispensable, since it is known. The meaning is: except a creation existing with the accompaniment of truth, while those who disbelieve turn away from what they were warned of, by what the creation with truth indicates.

The subject of the circumstantial clause is ﴿the heavens and the earth﴾, and the meaning is: We did not create them except in a state of their being accompanied by truth and the specification of a term for them. The turning away of those who disbelieve from what they were warned of, from the verses of the Qur'an that remind them of what is in the creation of the heavens and the earth of the accompaniment of truth.

The coordination of "and for a specified term" (wa-ajalin musamman) upon "in truth" is the coordination of the specific upon the general, for the sake of giving it importance, like the coordination of Gabriel and Michael upon His angels in His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and His angels and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98] in Surat al-Baqarah. This is because the indication that createdness implies acceptance of annihilation is a rational indication, so it is among what truth requires; and the exposure of the heavens and the earth to annihilation is evidence for the occurrence of the Resurrection, because the cessation of this world requires, by the dictates of wisdom, that another world, greater than it, succeed it, following the custom of the gradual progression of created beings toward perfection. The belief of the Dahriyyah (materialists) in the eternity of this world and its permanence was their greatest doubt in denying the Resurrection: ﴿And they say: There is only our life of this world; we die and we live, and nothing destroys us except time﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 24]. For them, time acts and is itself permanent, not perishing. So if they allowed the annihilation of this world, it would have been possible for them to descend to consider the proofs that require a second life. Thus the clause ﴿But those who disbelieve turn away from what they are warned of﴾ is connected to the exception in His saying "except in truth", meaning: they turn away from what they were warned of regarding the threat of the Day of Resurrection.

The returning pronoun of the relative clause has been omitted, because it is a pronoun in the accusative governed by "unthirū" (were warned). The meaning: from what they were warned of.

It is also permissible for "mā" to be a verbal-noun particle (maṣdariyyah), in which case no pronoun is to be estimated after it. The meaning then: turning away from their warning, so it encompasses every warning they were given.

The fronting of "from what they were warned of" before its governed element, which is "turn away" (muʿriḍūn), is for the sake of giving importance to what they were warned of, and this is followed by observing the rhyme (fāṣilah).

﴿Say: Have you considered those you invoke besides Allah? Show me what they have created from the earth, or do they have a share in the heavens? Bring me a Scripture before this, or some remnant of knowledge, if you are truthful﴾.

He moved on to the argument against the divinity (ilahiyyah) of their idols.

The clause ﴿Say: Have you considered those you invoke﴾ is a command to present the proof that refutes associating partners with Allah, which is the root of their misguidance.

This argument came in the form of debate (munazarah), in which the Prophet ﷺ confronted them with reasoning so as to compel them to admit their inability to counter his proof. In the same way, the argument continued three times after this, in the form of a challenge (ta'jiz) through the command in His words ﴿Show me what they have created from the earth, or do they have a share in the heavens. Bring me a Scripture﴾, and so on. The phrase ﴿Have you considered﴾ (a'ara'aytum) is an interrogative of confirmation (istifham taqriri), which is a metaphorical expression meaning "Inform me." His words in Surat al-An'am, ﴿Say: Have you considered, if the punishment of Allah comes upon you, or the Hour comes upon you, would you call upon other than Allah?﴾ [al-An'am: 40], have already passed.

His words ﴿Show me﴾ are an explicit statement of what the form of confirmation had implied by his words ﴿Have you considered those you invoke﴾. The clause ﴿Show me﴾ occupies the position of the second object of the verb "have you considered."

The imperative in ﴿Show me what they have created from the earth﴾ is used for ridicule and challenge (taskhir wa ta'jiz), and is a metaphor for negation: if they have created nothing from the earth, then you cannot show me anything that they created on the earth. This is one of the principal issues of debate, namely demanding that the claimant produce evidence for his claim.

"Madha" (what) here means "what is it that they created?" So "ma" is interrogative and "dha" means "alladhi" (that which). Originally it was a demonstrative noun that replaced the relative pronoun, and the original construction was "ma dha alladhi khalaqu," but it was shortened to the demonstrative. Omitting the relative pronoun is common in speech, and it may appear, as in His words, may He be exalted, ﴿Who is it that can intercede with Him?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255]. For this reason the grammarians said that "dha" after the interrogatives "ma" or "man" is in the position of the relative "ma."

The interrogative in "ma dha khalaqu" is one of denial (inkari). The clause "ma dha khalaqu" is a substitute (badal) for the clause "Show me."

The verb of seeing is suspended from acting (mu'allaq) by the interrogative "ma" following it. If none of the earth's creations were created by them, then it is invalid that they are gods, since the created beings lie outside their creation. And if it is invalid that they have any creation, it is invalid that they have any control over created beings, as He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Do they associate with Him what creates nothing, while they themselves are created, and they cannot help them, nor can they help themselves?﴾ [al-A'raf: 191], in Surat al-A'raf.

"Am" is a particle of transitional turning away (idrab intiqali). The interrogative that is implied after the disjunctive "am" is an interrogative of denial, meaning: they have no partnership with Allah in the heavens.

The negation of partnership is singled out with respect to the heavens, rather than the negation of creation, just as the negation of creation was singled out with respect to the earth. This is because the creatures of the earth are observed by people, and their development and coming-into-being are evident, and it is evident that what they invoke besides Allah has no least effect in bringing them into being. As for the heavenly beings, they are hidden from the eyes, and people have no familiarity with their appearance or development. So it is not fitting to argue from the lack of influence of the idols in bringing anything of them into being. But since the polytheists did not attribute any action to the idols except in the affairs of people on earth, such as bringing benefit or repelling harm, the argument was restricted, in negating their influence in the heavens, to denying that the idols have any partnership in heavenly affairs, because that negation is something they do not dispute.

A parallel to this verse has already appeared in Surat Fatir: ﴿Say: Have you considered your partners whom you invoke besides Allah?﴾ [Fatir: 40], and so on. Refer to that.

Then he moved from argument by observation and by admission to argument by true reports, with His words ﴿Bring me a Scripture before this﴾, and so on.

The clause ﴿Bring me a Scripture﴾ occupies the position of the second object of the verb "have you considered," and it is repeated just as the predicate of a subject may be multiplied. The basis of the argument is that it is a refutation of the claimant's assertion by the absence of any proof for his claim, and this is called silencing (ifham), as has passed. The meaning is: the negation that they have any proof for the divinity of the idols, neither through their influence on created beings nor through the statements of books. This is close to His words in Surat Fatir: ﴿Or have We given them a Scripture, so that they stand on clear evidence from it?﴾ [Fatir: 40].

By "Scripture" is meant any one of the written books. This is decisive against them, for they cannot claim that their idols are mentioned in the earlier Scriptures except for their refutation and their warning against worshipping them. Nothing is found in the Scriptures except one of two things: either the refutation of idol worship, as in the heavenly Scriptures, or no mention of them whatsoever. That this is what is meant is shown by His words after it, ﴿or some remnant of knowledge﴾.

The verb "bring" (ita') is used metaphorically for "produce," even if it is in their assembly, as has passed in His words, may He be exalted, ﴿So bring a surah like it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 23], in Surat al-Baqarah.

The reference in His words "before this" is to the Qur'an, because it is present in the minds of those who dispute with the Prophet, since it is recited to them repeatedly.

The reason for specifying the Scripture by the description that it be from before the Qur'an is so as to close off for them the door of counterfeiting, by which they might bring a book that is fabricated for them, just as they said: ﴿If we wished, we could say the like of this; this is nothing but the fables of the ancients﴾ [al-Anfal: 31].

"Athara" with a fatha on the hamza means the remnant of a thing. The meaning is: or a remnant that has survived with you, which you narrate from earlier people of knowledge, not written down in books. This is an expansion for them in the kinds of proof, so that their inability to bring anything of that kind would be more decisive against their claim.

His words "if you are truthful" are a stirring up and a silencing of them, in that they cannot bring a proof neither from the side of reason nor from the side of transmitted text, whether written or handed down. He, may He be exalted, said in Surat al-Qasas: ﴿And if they do not respond to you, then know that they only follow their own desires﴾ [al-Qasas: 50].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 46, verses 5–6:

﴿And who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah those who will not respond to him until the Day of Resurrection, while they are unaware of their calling?﴾ ﴿And when the people are gathered, they will be enemies to them and will deny their worship.﴾

This is an interjection in the midst of the argumentation. When Allah the Exalted commanded His Messenger ﷺ to argue with them by evidence, He turned the address toward him, marveling at their state and their misguidance, because His saying ﴿And when the people are gathered, they will be enemies to them﴾ etc. is only fitting as coming from the side of Allah.

And "man" (مَنِ) is interrogative, and the interrogation is one of denial and wonder.

The meaning: there is no one more astray and more wondrous in state than those who call upon other than Allah one who does not respond to their call; so he is at the furthest extreme of error.

The reason for this is that they went astray from the signs of God's oneness, claimed partners for Allah without any evidence, and chose as partners stones, which are the furthest of existing things from accepting the attributes of creation, formation and disposal. Then they call upon them in their calamities, while they witness that they neither hear, nor see, nor respond. Then they heard the verses of the Qur'an clarifying to them the reminder about the deficiencies of their gods, yet they did not take heed by them and claimed that it was manifest magic. So their error was at the furthest extreme of error.

As for "those who will not respond" (﴿مَن لا يَسْتَجِيبُ﴾), it refers to the idols. The idols are expressed by the relative pronoun specific to rational beings, treating the inanimate as rational, since the attribute of heedlessness, which is ascribed to the people of knowledge, is ascribed to them. Also, because it has become common in Arabic speech to treat them as rational, the Qur'an frequently follows this usage. Similar to this is the use of the plural pronouns for rational beings in His saying "wa-hum" (وهم) and "ghafilun" (غافِلُونَ), though they refer back to "man la yastajibu" (whoever does not respond).

Making the Day of Resurrection the limit for the non-response is a metonymy for the extension of the duration of the world's existence. The end of the worldly life is expressed as "the Day of Resurrection" because the one addressed by the report is the Messenger ﷺ and the believers, as you know, and they will be established on the Day of Resurrection.

The two pronouns in "akanu" (أكانُوا) in both places may refer back to those who call upon other than Allah, for the polytheists will be hostile to their idols on the Day of Resurrection, finding them among the causes of their wretchedness. They may also refer back to "man la yastajibu lahu" (one who does not respond to him), for the idols may be given life on that day, so they speak of disavowing their worshippers and their worship of them. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And on the day He gathers them and what they worship besides Allah, He will say, "Did you lead these servants of Mine astray, or did they themselves stray from the way?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 17] ﴿They will say, "Exalted are You! It was not for us to take any allies besides You, but You gave them and their fathers enjoyment until they forgot the remembrance, and they were a people ruined."﴾ [al-Furqan: 18] ﴿So they will have denied you in what you say﴾ [al-Furqan: 19].

It is also possible that His saying ﴿they will be enemies to them and will deny their worship﴾ is a eloquent metaphor (al-tashbih al-baligh), because the idols resemble enemies and deniers of worship in indicating what leads to their wretchedness and falsehood, as in His saying: ﴿And they added to them nothing but ruin﴾ [Hud: 101].

The clause "And when the people are gathered" etc. is conjoined to what precedes it because of the relevance of mentioning the Day of Resurrection.

A marvel of the Qur'an's variety is the distribution of the referents of the pronouns in this verse despite their similarity in wording; this falls under the figure of combining and separating (al-jam' ma'a al-tafriq), and it is more subtle.

This is a conjunction (*'atf*) on the clause "Who is more astray than one who calls upon other than Allah, one who will not respond to him" [al-Ahqaf: 5]. You have already understood that this passage is presented as an enumeration of the aspects of their extreme misguidance. The verses of the Qur'an are recited to them morning and evening, clarifying for them the proofs that the idols lack the attributes of divinity. Yet they do not reflect upon them, and the verses guide them toward the truth. So they deceive themselves, claiming that what they understood from them is a magical influence, and that the verses are magic. They were not content with this, but added further slander by claiming that it is "clear" (*mubin*), meaning that its being magic is evident.

This is a transition to refuting another of their errors, namely the error of denying the Qur'an. It is therefore connected to His saying, "Ha Mim. The revelation of the Book is from Allah" [al-Ahqaf: 1], and so on.

His saying "those who disbelieved" (*alladhina kafaru*) is an explicit noun in the place where a pronoun would be expected (*idhar fi maqam al-idmar*), in order to record their disbelief against them and to indicate that disbelief is the cause of their saying this.

The *lam* in His saying "for the truth" (*lil-haqq*) is the *lam* of cause (*lam al-'illah*), and it is not the *lam* that transmits the verb of saying to its object of speech. The meaning is: some of the disbelievers said to one another, concerning those who believed and whose faith was deferred (*man ujjila iymanuhum*), that...

"The truth" (*al-haqq*) refers to the verses. He turned away from the pronoun referring to the verses to the explicit word "the truth," to draw attention to the fact that they are true, and that labeling them as magic is a great slander. His saying "when it came to them" (*lamma ja'ahum*) specifies the time of their statement: they say this immediately upon hearing the verses and whenever they come to them, that is, without reflection or deliberation.

[p. 14]

This is a transition (*idrab intiqal*, a shift marked by a particle meaning "rather/but") to another kind of their misguided speech.

In shifting to this new topic, he used the form of *idrab* rather than coordinating with *wa* (and). This is because *idrab* indicates that the matter he is moving to has a closer connection with what came before. The meaning is: "Set aside their saying, 'It is manifest magic,' and listen to what is more astonishing, which is their saying *iftarahu* ('he invented it'), that is, that he invented its attribution to God, and they did not mean by it magic."

The interrogative (*istifham*) that is understood after *am* (or) is an interrogative of denial (*istifham inkari*) directed at their assertion.

The negation implied by the interrogative of denial applies to the cause of the denial, that is, the Qur'an being fabricated, and does not apply to the attribution of the saying to them, because it issues from them. What is negated is the alleged fabrication.

The object pronoun in *iftarahu* refers either to *al-haqq* (the truth) in His saying ﴿Those who disbelieved say of the truth﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 7], or to the Qur'an, which is known from the context. The meaning is: he invented the Qur'an and claimed that it is revelation from God.

The Messenger ﷺ was commanded to answer their statement with something that uproots it at its root. So His saying, "*Qul*" (Say), is a sentence functioning as a response to a dialogue, since it stands in opposition to the report of their saying. This has been discussed earlier in His saying ﴿They said, "Will You place therein one who causes corruption therein?"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 30] at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The fabrication was posited with the particle *in* (if), whose function is that its condition is usually of rare occurrence. This indicates that it is posited in a situation that contains evidence which uproots the condition from its base.

*Shay'an* (anything) is in the accusative as the object of the verb *tamlikun* (you control), meaning: anything that can be controlled, that is, can be done, and what is intended is: some measure of repelling. So you are not able to ward off from me anything that comes upon me from God. The meaning of "I do not control anything" was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿Say, "Who could prevent God at all if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary...?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 17], in Surat al-'Uqud.

The implied meaning is: "If I had invented it, God would have punished me with a punishment that you could not turn back." So His saying ﴿so you cannot control for me anything from God﴾ is evidence of the implied answer in the sentence, by way of implication (*iltizam*), because the meaning of "you cannot control for me" is "you are not able to repel God's harm from me." It therefore implies that the meaning is: "If I had invented it, God would have punished me, and you could not repel His punishment."

Know that the common usage of "I do not control anything for him" and similar expressions is for the verb of control to be attributed to the one who is expected to repel, with the *lam* complement attached to the verb of control, as in His saying ﴿I do not control for myself any benefit or harm﴾ [al-A'raf: 188], and His saying ﴿and I cannot avail you anything against God﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]. Or it may be attributed to a general agent, as in ﴿Say, "Who could prevent God at all if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary...?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 17]. The attribution of the verb of control in this verse to the addressees, who are the enemies of the Prophet ﷺ, is not because they are expected to repel anything from him, since they have set themselves up in the position of judge over the Prophet ﷺ and have decided that he invented the Qur'an. Their situation is that of one who claims he can thwart God's will, in the manner of mockery.

Know also that the connection (*mulazamah*) between the condition and its answer in His saying ﴿If I had invented it, you cannot control for me anything from God﴾ is that God does not allow anyone to convey to people anything from God that He did not command him to convey. The Qur'an has indicated this in His saying ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings, We would have seized him by the right hand, then cut from him the aorta, and none of you could have held Us off from him﴾ [al-Haqqah: 44–47]. Perhaps the wisdom behind this is that fabricating against God leads to great corruption by which the order of creation is disrupted, and God is jealous over His creatures. This is unlike other sins brought about by injustices and mischief on earth, because those are acts whose corruption is known and is not hidden from people, so they repel it with whatever strength, power, cunning, or compromise they can. As for fabricating against God, it puts people in confusion about how to receive it, so God does not allow it and removes it.

The sentence ﴿He is most knowing of what you spread into it﴾ is a substitute of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*) for the sentence ﴿so you cannot control for me anything from God﴾, because the sentence ﴿so you cannot control for me﴾ includes the meaning that God does not approve of anyone fabricating against Him. That requires that He is more knowing than they are of the state of one who reports from God that He sent him and of what he conveys from God. That is what they engage in: slander, disparagement, and describing him as a sorcerer, a fabricator, or a madman. Therefore the relative *ma* (what) may refer to the Qur'an, indicated by the apparent pronoun in *iftarahu*, or to the Messenger ﷺ, indicated by the hidden pronoun in *iftarahu*, or to the totality of the states of the Messenger ﷺ, which is indicated by the variety of their discourse. The complement of the superlative (*ism al-tafdil*) is omitted, meaning: he is more knowing than you. *Al-ifadah* (spreading) in speech means engaging in it and increasing it, and it is derived from *fa'a al-ma'* (the water flowed), when it flowed. From it comes the expression *hadith mustafid* (a widely spread report), meaning famous and widespread. The meaning is: He is most knowing of the state of what you spread into it.

[p. 15]

The sentence ﴿Sufficient is He as witness between me and you﴾ is a substitute of inclusion for the sentence ﴿He is most knowing of what you spread into it﴾, because the report that He is more knowing than them of the reality of what they spread into includes the meaning of entrusting the judgment between Him and them to God, the Exalted. This is a threat to them, a warning against engaging in falsehood, and a warning of punishment.

*Al-shahid* (the witness) is the one who testifies, that is, the one who reports the reality. Here it means the judge who judges by what He knows of our state, as indicated by His saying "between me and you," because judgment takes place between two adversaries, and testimony is not between them, but is for one of them. He, the Exalted, said ﴿And We bring you as a witness against these﴾ [al-Nisa: 41].

The attribution of the two descriptions "the Forgiving, the Merciful" to Him, the Exalted, is required by what is contained in His saying ﴿Sufficient is He as witness between me and you﴾ of threat and warning. It is an indirect call to them to desist from what they are engaged in of vain talk.

[Page 16]

The command is repeated, that he should say what is a proof against them, as you have already learned in the explanation of His words: ﴿Say: Have you considered those you invoke besides God?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 4] and what follows.

This is a response to what their words "He has invented it" (*iftarahu*) contained: they denied that his truthfulness in what he brought as a message from God was possible, a denial that led them to attribute to the Messenger ﷺ the fabrication of lies against God. The verse was not joined by conjunction to the sentence ﴿Say: If I have invented it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 8] because the aim is to escalate the refutation of them from one rebuttal to a stronger one. Thus this resembles a repetition and reiteration. After it comes His words ﴿Say: Have you considered, if it is from God and you have disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 10]. A parallel to this is in Surat al-Mu'minun: ﴿Nay, they said the like of what the former ones said﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 81], down to ﴿Say: To whom belongs the earth and whatever is in it, if you know?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 84], and His words ﴿Say: Who is the Lord of the seven heavens?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 86], and His words ﴿Say: In whose hand is the dominion of all things?﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 88], and so on.

*Bid'* (with a kasra on the *ba'* and a sukun on the *dal*) means *badi'*, "original, unprecedented," like *khiff* meaning *khafif* ("light"). Imru' al-Qays said:

*Page 17*

*The light youth slips from the back of his saddle-horse*

From the same root comes *khill* meaning *khalil* ("close friend"). So *bid'* is an assimilated adjective (*sifah mushabbahah*) in the sense of *badi'*. Among God's names, exalted is He, is *al-Badi'*, the Originator of things and the One who brings them into existence. The meaning is: "I am not one who introduces something that had not existed among the messengers."

The *min* in ﴿min al-rusul﴾ is *ibtida'iyyah* (the "min" of origin/starting point), meaning: "I am not someone coming from among them as a novelty unlike them." Just as you have heard that the earlier messengers reported that God's message was sent to them, so too am I. Why then do they wonder at my call?

This verse is suitable for refuting the Christians of our time who attacked his prophethood with slanders that have no source except misleading and deceiving their common people, because those who attack him are not so foolish that their falsehood would be hidden from them. Examples are their claim that he married women, or that he fought those who disbelieved, or that he loved Zaynab bint Jahsh.

His words ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾ are a completion (*tatmim*) of His words ﴿I am not something new among the messengers﴾. It stands in the position of a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiradh*). The polytheists used to ask the Prophet ﷺ about unseen matters mockingly. One of them would say, when his camel had strayed, "Where is my camel?" Another would say, "Who is my father?" or something similar. So God commanded the Messenger ﷺ to inform them that he does not know what will be done to him or to them, that is, in this world. This is the meaning of the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I have no power to benefit or harm myself except as God wills. Had I known the unseen, I would have acquired much good, and no evil would have touched me﴾ [al-A'raf: 188].

For this reason His words ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾ are an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*) and a completion of what is in His words ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾. The most he knows is to follow what God informs him of. So it is a specification of its generality. Among such things are his knowledge that he is a messenger from God, that the polytheists are in the Fire, and that there is a resurrection after death. Also, that he would migrate to a land of palm trees between two lava fields, and His words, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed We have granted you a clear victory﴾ [al-Fath: 1], and similar things that return to what God informed him of. So leave aside what some exegetes have extended here regarding the intended meaning of ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾, and regarding whether it is abrogated (*mansukhah*) or decisive (*muhkamah*), and regarding the ruling on the abrogation of a report.

The reason for the conjunction of "nor with you" (*wa la bikum*) to "with me" (*bi*) by inserting the negative particle *la* is that although both are dependent on the verb of the relative clause of *ma* (the relative pronoun), there is no negation in the relative clause. Why then did he not say: "what will be done with me and with you"? Because the relative pronoun and its clause, when they became the object of the negated verb in His words "and I do not know," the negation covered what lies within the scope of that negated verb. So the negation became inclusive of all of them, and it was good to introduce the negative particle before the conjoined noun, just as it is good for the particle *bi'* (which is normally added) to govern a negated noun conjoined to the noun of *inna*, when that noun is affirmed, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Have they not seen that God, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33]. This is because the *an* (that) which governs it occurs in the predicate of the negation, namely "Have they not seen." Likewise is the addition of *min* in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book, nor the polytheists, would not like that any good should be sent down upon you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 105]. Here *khayr* ("good") is the object of the verb *yunazzal* ("be sent down"), which is affirmative, but since their desire for its descent is negated, the descent becomes like something negated in their eyes.

The conjunction of ﴿And I am but a plain warner﴾ to the sentence ﴿I am not something new among the messengers﴾ is because it is the purpose for which the speech is directed, unlike His words ﴿And I do not know what will be done with me or with you﴾.

The meaning is: "I am but a plain warner, not a fabricator." So the restriction (*qasr*) is a relative restriction (*qasr idafi*), and it is a restriction by reversal (*qasr qalb*), to reject their words "He has invented it."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 46, verse 10:

﴿Say: Have you considered? If it is from Allah and you have disbelieved in it, and a witness from the Children of Israel has testified to its like and believed while you have been arrogant, [then what?] Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾

The matter is repeated, with another argument by which he tells them, perhaps it will turn them back to the truth, after what preceded in His saying ﴿Say: Have you considered what you invoke besides Allah﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 4] the verse, and His saying ﴿Say: If I had invented it, then you would not have power for me against Allah at all﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 8], and His saying ﴿Say: I am not an innovation among the messengers﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9] the verse.

This is a gradual leading of them to the truth through the stages of reflection. He began by showing them that what they deemed impossible, that a messenger should come from Allah, is not impossible, since he was not the first of mankind to come with a message from Allah. Then he followed this with: if we suppose that the Qur'an is from Allah and you have disbelieved in it, how will your state be before Allah, exalted is He?

He inserted into this that if a witness from the People of the Book testified to the occurrence of messages and the sending of scriptures to the messengers, and believed in my message, how would your falling short of his rank be, when a Book has come to you and you have turned away from it? This is like His saying ﴿Or you say: If the Book had been revealed to us, we would surely have been better guided than them﴾ [al-An'am: 157]. This is a stirring of resolve.

The parallel of this verse is the verse in Surah Fussilat: ﴿Say: Have you considered? If it is from Allah and you have disbelieved in it, who is more astray than one who is in extreme opposition?﴾ [Fussilat: 52], except that this one includes His saying ﴿and a witness from the Children of Israel has testified﴾. The polytheists had associations with some of the Jews in Mecca, and dealings with many of them in trade in Medina and Khaybar. When the call of the Prophet ﷺ became apparent, they would ask whomever they met among the Jews about matters of religions and messengers, and the Jews would inevitably inform the polytheists of some reports about the message of Musa and his Book, and how Allah made him prevail over Pharaoh.

Although the Jews do not acknowledge the message of Muhammad ﷺ, they speak of the message of Musa ('alayhi al-salam) in terms similar to the situation of the Prophet ﷺ with his people, and in it there is sufficient to repel their denial of his message.

The interrogative in ﴿Have you considered?﴾ is an affirmative interrogative for rebuke, and the two objects of "ara'aytum" are omitted.

The estimate is: "Have you considered yourselves to be wrongdoers?" The hidden pronoun in ﴿If it is﴾ refers to the Qur'an, known from the context, or to "what is revealed to me" in His earlier saying ﴿I only follow what is revealed to me﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9]. The clause "and you have disbelieved in it" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun of "ara'aytum". It may also be coordinated with the conditional verb. Likewise the clause ﴿and a witness from the Children of Israel has testified﴾, because the content of both clauses is actual and so does not fall within the scope of the condition. The response of the condition is omitted, indicated by the context of the dispute. The estimate is: "Do you then see yourselves in error?"

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to the omitted clause that is the response of the condition, and it is also a causal explanation. The meaning is: Do you think that if it becomes clear that the Qur'an is revelation from Allah while you have disbelieved in that, and a witness has testified to the reality of that, you will be certain that Allah has not guided you because you are wrongdoers, and that Allah does not guide wrongdoers?

The two pronouns in "kana" and "mithlihi" refer to the Qur'an, which has been mentioned several times, in His saying ﴿The revelation of the Book from Allah﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 2] and His saying ﴿Bring me a Book from before this﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 4].

The clause "wa-istakbartum" is coordinated with the clause "wa-shahida shahid" etc., and the clause "wa-shahida shahid" is coordinated with the clause "in kana min 'indi Allah."

The "mithl" means the like and the similar in a quality or an act. The pronoun of "mithlihi" refers to the Qur'an, so the word "mithlihi" here may be taken as explicit description, meaning: similar to the Qur'an in what they denied of what the Qur'an contains, such as the oneness of Allah and the affirmation of resurrection. That "mithl" is the Torah or the Psalms among the books of the Children of Israel at that time.

It may also be taken that "mithl" is a kinaya (allusion) for what the word "mithl" is attached to, so the word "mithl" is in the position of an inserted word in the manner of the Arabic saying: "Someone like you does not stint," and as is one of the two interpretations of His saying ﴿There is nothing like unto Him﴾ [al-Shura: 11]. The meaning then is: and a witness testified to the truthfulness of the Qur'an in what it contains.

The pronoun of "mithlihi" may also refer to the preceding speech by way of interpreting it as "what was mentioned," meaning: like what was mentioned, that it is from Allah and that it is not an innovation among the books of the messengers.

Thus what is meant by ﴿a witness from the Children of Israel﴾ is an unspecified witness, i.e., any witness, because the speech is an informing of them about what they were asking about with the Jews. On this basis al-Sha'bi and Masruq interpreted, and Ibn 'Abd al-Barr preferred it in al-Isti'ab in the biography of 'Abd Allah ibn Salam. The address in "ara'aytum" and what follows is directed to the polytheists of Mecca.

Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatada, Mujahid and 'Ikrima said: what is meant by ﴿a witness from the Children of Israel﴾ is 'Abd Allah ibn Salam. al-Tirmidhi narrated from 'Abd Allah ibn Salam that he said: "Verses of the Book of Allah were revealed concerning me: ﴿and a witness from the Children of Israel has testified﴾, the verse."

Similar to the saying of Qatada, Mujahid and 'Ikrima is narrated from Ibn Zayd, Malik ibn Anas and Sufyan al-Thawri. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, in the chapter on the virtue of 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, there occurs the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Yusuf from Malik from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas who said: "Concerning him this verse was revealed: ﴿and a witness from the Children of Israel has testified to its like﴾, the verse." 'Abd Allah ibn Yusuf said: "I do not know whether Malik said: the verse, or in the hadith."

Masruq said: "It is not Ibn Salam, because he embraced Islam in Medina and the surah is Meccan." al-Sha'bi said the same. It is possible that the verse was revealed in Medina and was ordered to be placed in Surah al-Ahqaf, and on this basis the address in "ara'aytum" and what follows is to the People of the Book in Medina and its surroundings. In my view, it is possible that this is an informing from Allah to His Messenger ﷺ about what would come to pass of the faith of 'Abd Allah ibn Salam, so he would be what is meant by ﴿a witness from the Children of Israel﴾, even though the verse is Meccan.

The apparent meaning is that verses like this one are what emboldened the polytheists to deny the descent of revelation upon Musa and other messengers, so they said ﴿We will never believe in this Qur'an nor in that which is before it﴾ [Saba': 31], and they said ﴿Allah did not send down anything upon a human﴾ [al-An'am: 91], when they knew that the proof had become binding upon them by the descent of the earlier books before the Qur'an.

The clause ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ is a causal explanation for the omitted speech indicated by what precedes it, as you have known just now, meaning: you have gone astray with an error for which there is no hope of its removal, because you are wrongdoers. ﴿Indeed Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people.﴾ This is a recording against them of their wronging of themselves.

In the conditional, the particle (in) is used, which by nature belongs to a condition whose occurrence is not certain, in accordance with the state of the addressees, to coax their wild steed down so that they will come down to reflection and dialogue.

[p. 22]

This is another instance of the false arguments of the polytheists, a error whose source is self-admiration and conceit in their own religion. So they inferred that there is no good in Islam because those who hastened to embrace it were the weak among the people, whom they regarded as inferior to themselves. They are the ones who said ﴿Are these the ones on whom Allah has bestowed favour from among us?﴾ [al-An'am: 53], as was mentioned earlier in al-An'am. This is similar to the words of Noah's people: ﴿And we do not see you followed except by those who are the lowest of us, in immature judgment﴾ [Hud: 27]. Its connection to what precedes it is that it is one of the effects of their arrogance, so it fits His saying "and you were arrogant."

The lam in His saying "for those who believed" (لِلَّذِينَ آمَنُوا) is the lam of causation (lam al-ta'lil), connected to an omitted element that is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "those who disbelieved." Its estimated meaning is: "singling them out" or "intending," like the lam in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they said to their brothers when they traveled through the land or were raiders, "If they had remained with us, they would not have died or been killed"﴾ [Al 'Imran: 156], and His saying in the preceding verse: ﴿Those who disbelieved said to the truth when it came to them, "This is evident magic"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 7].

It is not the lam that makes the verb of saying transitive to the one addressed by the saying, as in ﴿Did I not tell you that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ [al-Kahf: 72], which is called the lam of communication (lam al-tabligh).

The hidden pronoun in (كانَ, kana, "it was") refers back to what the pronoun in ﴿if it is from Allah﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 10] refers to, namely the Qur'an, understood from the context, or to "what is revealed to me."

Al-sabq (precedence) is applied to obtaining something before another obtains it, and is likened to the swiftest arrival among racers. What is meant is taking up what the Qur'an brought of beliefs and deeds.

The pronoun of the third person in His saying "they preceded us" (سَبَقُونا) refers to something not mentioned in the verse, but it is mentioned in the speech of those who disbelieved, which the verse relates. They meant by it the first believers among the oppressed, such as Bilal, 'Ammar ibn Yasir, 'Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Sumayya, and Zinnira (spelled with a Z, a dotted letter with a kasra, an N with a kasra and shadda, lengthened, and then a R, an undotted letter), a Byzantine (Rumi) slave woman who was among the earliest to embrace Islam, among those whom the polytheists tortured, and among those whom Abu Bakr al-Siddiq freed.

From 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr: the nobles of Quraysh said, "If what Muhammad brought were good, Zinnira would not have preceded us to it." That is, it is among the sayings they uttered, which the Qur'an gathered into the pronoun in "they preceded us."

* * *

﴿And since they have not been guided by it, they will say, "This is an ancient falsehood."﴾

This is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿And those who disbelieved said to those who believed...﴾, that is: with their claims they have exhausted the aspects of criticism of the Qur'an. They said, "It is evident magic," they said, "He has fabricated it," and they said, ﴿If it had been good, they would not have preceded us to it﴾. There remained for them to say that it is ﴿an ancient falsehood﴾.

Allah has indicated that all their claims arise from their disbelief and arrogance, by His saying ﴿Those who disbelieved said﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 7], and His saying ﴿and you disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 10], and His saying ﴿and you were arrogant﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 10], and His saying ﴿And since they have not been guided by it﴾ and the rest of the verse.

Since their statements were aimed at one purpose, which is denying the Messenger (ﷺ), distributing their causes among the different statements indicates that all of them are causes for all of them.

[p. 23]

The pronoun in (بِهِ, "by it") refers to the Qur'an, and the demonstrative refers back to it.

The meaning of the verse: since their guidance has not been achieved by the Qur'an in the past, they will continue to say of it, "It is an ancient falsehood," since there is no hope of their giving up their misguidance in the future. Since (إذْ, idh) is an adverb of past time, and here it is added to a clause that occurs in past time, as the negation with the particle (لَمْ, lam) requires, it is determined that the report about them, that they "will say this is a falsehood," means that they will say it in the future. This indicates that they were also saying that in the past, because their saying that is among the variations of their misguided statements that are related about them in other surahs revealed before this surah. So the meaning of "they will say" (فَسَيَقُولُونَ) is that they will persist in this statement in the future.

Thus the future tense expresses continuity and repetition of this statement, like His saying, may He be exalted, relating the words of Abraham: ﴿And he said, "Indeed, I am going to my Lord; He will guide me"﴾ [al-Saffat: 99], for He had already guided him before. He only meant that He would continue his guidance to me.

So the aim is not for Allah to inform His Messenger (ﷺ) that they "will say this" while they did not say it in the past, for such information would be of no benefit. And since it has been related that they said what is synonymous with this in many verses preceding this verse, and that they do not desist from it, there is no need to estimate a omitted verb to which (إذْ) is attached.

Since the adverb is placed before its governing element in the speech, it takes on the meaning of a conditional, and this is a usage found in speech, and common with (إذْ). For this reason the fa' (فَ) entered its response here in His saying "so they will say." It is also possible that (إذْ) is for causation, and (إذْ) is connected to "they will say," and the fa' does not prevent what follows it from governing what precedes it, according to the verified view. The sentence was arranged in this way only to convey these rhetorical particularities: the waw is for conjunction, and the conjoined element carries the meaning of a condition, and the fa' is for the response of the condition. The original sentence is: "And they will say, 'This is an ancient falsehood,' since they have not been guided by it!"

This explanation follows what Ibn al-Hajib chose in his Amali, rather than what the author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) held, for he made a forced and unconvincing effort regarding it.

[p. 24]

﴿And before it was the Book of Moses, a guide and a mercy. And this is a Book confirming it in Arabic tongue, to warn those who wronged and as good tidings for the doers of good.﴾

He (Allah) follows the refutation of their idle claims, which attack the Qur'an, with this statement, which adds further refutation of their assertions by reminding them of a counterpart to the Qur'an and a like of it among the Books of Allah, the Exalted. It is well known among them, and it is the Torah. This comes with praise for the Qur'an and its distinction, and with rebuke of them, since they deprived themselves of benefiting from it. This verse is joined to the one before it because they are connected in refuting their claims, and because it refers back to His saying, ﴿And a witness from the Children of Israel testified to its like﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 10], as was mentioned earlier.

In His saying, ﴿And before it was the Book of Moses﴾, there is a refutation of their denial that Allah would reveal to Muhammad (ﷺ). Revelation is a divine practice that preceded it, well known, the most famous example of which is the Book of Moses, meaning the Torah. They had already received news of his prophethood from the Jews.

The pronoun in ﴿مِن قَبْلِهِ﴾ ("before it") refers to the Qur'an.

The fronting of ﴿مِن قَبْلِهِ﴾ ("before it") is for emphasis on this report, because it is the focal point of the sentence.

The Torah is referred to as ﴿كِتابُ مُوسى﴾ ("the Book of Moses") by way of an idafa (construct phrase), rather than by its proper name, the Torah. This is because the attribution to Moses's name indicates that it was a book sent down to a human being, just as the Qur'an was sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ). This alludes to the basis of the conclusion drawn from analogizing the Qur'an to the Book of Moses through resemblance in all respects.

﴿إمامًا ورَحْمَةً﴾ ("a guide and a mercy") are two circumstantial accusatives (ḥāl) of "the Book of Moses". They may also be two circumstantial accusatives of Moses, and the two meanings are mutually implicated.

Imam (leader, guide) is literally that thing which the agent takes as a measure for the action of something else. It is commonly used for exemplar (qudwa). Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿وَاجْعَلْنَا لِلْمُتَّقِينَ إِمَامًا﴾ ("and make us leaders for the righteous") [al-Furqan: 74]. The origin of this usage is a metaphor (isti'ara) that has become like a literal meaning. The term imam was borrowed for the Book of Moses because it guides to what must be acted upon, so it is like one who guides and admonishes. Moses is also an imam in the sense of exemplar.

Rahma (mercy) is the verbal noun of the attribute of the merciful one. It is one of the attributes of human beings: a tenderness in the soul that prompts the pursuit of good for whomever it reaches. Describing the Book with it is a metaphor (isti'ara), since it is a cause of benefit for those who follow it, through the means of good it contains in this world and the Hereafter.

Describing the Book with the verbal noun is an intensification (mubalagha) within the metaphor. Moses is also a mercy through his message, just as Muhammad (ﷺ) was described with this in His saying: ﴿وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَاكَ إِلَّا رَحْمَةً لِّلْعَالَمِينَ﴾ ("And We did not send you except as a mercy to the worlds") [al-Anbiya: 107].

His saying ﴿وَهَذَا كِتَابٌ مُّصَدِّقٌ﴾ ("And this is a Book confirming") and so on is what is being compared with the Book of Moses.

The reference to the Qur'an by "this" (hadha) is because it is present in mention, so it is like one present in essence.

Muṣaddiq (confirmer) means one who informs of the truthfulness of another. The object of muṣaddiq is omitted so that it includes all the heavenly Books. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿مُصَدِّقًا لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ﴾ ("confirming what is before it") [al-Ahqaf: 30]. That is, it informs of the rightness of all the aims that the earlier heavenly Books brought. This is a great praise of the Qur'an, that it encompassed everything in the heavenly Books, and came as a sufficiency for them and as a clarifier of what is in them.

Tasdiq (confirmation) implies that it is a judge over what they differed about, and over what was distorted in their understanding. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿مُصَدِّقًا لِّمَا بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ مِنَ الْكِتَابِ وَمُهَيْمِنًا عَلَيْهِ﴾ ("confirming what is before it of the Book and a guardian over it") [al-Ma'ida: 48].

He adds further praise by describing it as ﴿لِسَانًا عَرَبِيًّا﴾ ("in Arabic tongue"), meaning an Arabic language, for it is the most eloquent of languages, the most penetrating into the souls of listeners, and the most beloved of languages to people. It is more noble, more eloquent, and more expressive than the language in which the Book of Moses came, and than the language in which his followers, the people of the Gospels, spoke and recorded.

The word ﴿لِسَانًا﴾ ("tongue") is included (idmaj, incorporation) to indicate that what is meant by its Arabness is the Arabic of its words, not the Arabness of its morals and teachings. This is because the morals of the Arabs at that time were a mixture of good and bad. When Islam came, it removed the bad from them. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "I was only sent to complete noble character." 

The use of tongue (lisan) for language became dominant, because the noblest use of the tongue is speech. Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿وَمَا أَرْسَلْنَا مِن رَّسُولٍ إِلَّا بِلِسَانِ قَوْمِهِ﴾ ("And We did not send any messenger except with the tongue of his people") [Ibrahim: 4], and He said: ﴿فَإِنَّمَا يَسَّرْنَاهُ بِلِسَانِكَ﴾ ("So We have only made it easy in your tongue") [Maryam: 97].

His saying ﴿لِتُنذِرَ الَّذِينَ ظَلَمُوا﴾ ("to warn those who wronged") may be connected to ﴿مُّصَدِّقًا لِّسَانًا عَرَبِيًّا﴾ ("confirming in Arabic tongue"), because what precedes it includes warning and glad tidings. The better view is that it is connected to the sense of guidance contained in "a Book" (kitab), which includes warning and glad tidings. This is better, so that ﴿لِتُنذِرَ﴾ ("to warn") is a cause for the Book in terms of its attribute and state.

Those who wronged are the polytheists: ﴿إِنَّ الشِّرْكَ لَظُلْمٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("Indeed, association [of others with Allah] is great injustice") [Luqman: 13]. Included with them are those believers who wronged themselves. For this reason, the phrase is contrasted with "the doers of good," who are the pious believers, because the intended meaning is wronging oneself, and its opposite is goodness (ihsan).

Warning has degrees, and glad tidings likewise.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir, al-Bazzi from Ibn Kathir, and Ya'qub read ﴿لِتُنذِرَ﴾ with a feminine (taʾ) prefix, addressing the Messenger (ﷺ). Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 46, verses 13–14:

﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast — there will be no fear concerning them, nor will they grieve.﴾ ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise, abiding therein eternally, as a reward for what they used to do.﴾ This is a explanatory resumption (isti'naf bayani), in which the explicit mention has given priority to the side of the believers among those listening to the Qur'an. For when they heard the good tidings, they looked forward to learning the description of the good tidings and the specification of the doers of good (al-muhsinin), so that they might place themselves in their proper positions. They were answered that the good tidings are the negation of fear and grief for them, that they are the companions of Paradise, and that the doers of good are those who said, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remained steadfast in their deeds. By its implication, there is an allusion (ta'rid) to those who wronged, for in the phrase "Those are the companions of Paradise" there is the implication of restriction (mafhum al-qasr).

Their definition by way of the relative clause (al-mawsuliyya), with what the relative clause indicates of the cause of their honor with Allah, is because they combined good conduct toward their Lord through affirming His oneness, fearing Him, and worshipping Him; and this is what is indicated by "said, 'Our Lord is Allah'," together with good conduct toward themselves, which is the meaning of "then remained steadfast."

In the relative clause, the verb "qalu" (they said) is used to concisely express the content said and its sufficiency from saying, "they acknowledged Allah alone and obeyed Him." The meaning is that they said it and believed its meaning, since the norm in speech is truthfulness, and they acted upon it, since the norm is the conformity of action to belief.

"Thumma" (then) indicates gradual sequence of rank (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), which is ascent and progression, for maintaining steadfastness is more difficult than attaining faith, because it requires repeated vigilance over the self. As for faith, reflection necessitates it and its belief arises at once, not requiring renewed attention. This is the aspect of rank-based sequence from one standpoint, although faith is higher in degree than action, insofar as it is a condition for the validity of action. For this reason, He, may He be exalted, uses "thumma," which indicates sequence, in His saying: ﴿But what will explain to you what the steep path is? It is the freeing of a neck﴾ [al-Balad: 12] up to His saying ﴿and then he became of those who believed﴾ [al-Balad: 17]. The two considerations differ according to the differing context in which speech is directed, as becomes apparent upon reflection here and there. A parallel to this was mentioned earlier in Surah Fussilat.

The entry of the "fa" (so) upon the predicate of the relative clause, which is "fa la khawfun 'alayhim" (then there is no fear concerning them), is because the relative clause is treated as a conditional clause, as if it were said: "If they say, 'Our Lord is Allah,' and then remain steadfast, then there is no fear concerning them." Similar to this is frequent in the Qur'an. It thus conveys that this is the cause of their security from fear and grief.

"'Alayhim" (concerning them) is the predicate of "khawf" (fear), meaning: no fear will settle upon them, strike them, or reach them.

The placing of the subject before the verbal predicate in His saying "wa la hum yahzanun" (nor will they grieve) is for restricting the subject to the predicate, like the saying: "I did not say this" (ma ana qultu hadha), meaning that grief is negated for them and not for others. By "others" is meant those who have not characterized themselves by faith and steadfastness, in the degrees of disbelief and disobedience. Thus the genus of fear is established for all others, according to the degrees of anticipating punishment, even in a state of trepidation about not having their intercession accepted and about being deprived of the outpourings of Allah, may He be exalted.

Their being brought to mind by the demonstrative "Ula'ika" (those) in His saying "Ula'ika ashab al-Jannah" (Those are the companions of Paradise) serves to alert that they are deserving of what follows by way of information about them after the demonstrative, because of the attributes mentioned before the demonstrative, as was previously mentioned in His saying ﴿Those are upon guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 5] at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

"Ashab al-Jannah" (companions of Paradise) is more indicative of exclusive association with Paradise than saying "Ula'ika fi al-Jannah" (those are in Paradise) or "Ula'ika lahumu al-Jannah" (for them is Paradise), because of the meaning of exclusivity in "ashab" and also in the construct form.

His saying ﴿as a reward for what they used to do﴾ explicitly states what was derived from the causal relative clause in the predicate, and from the demonstrative's indication of their worthiness for what follows, and what the descriptor "ashab" conveys and what the construct form conveys. This is part of the complete care in praising them.

Some of the exegetes sought the reason why this verse follows the one before it. Al-Qurtubi reports from al-Qushayri that the connection between the passages lies in showing that it is not far-fetched for some people to respond to the Prophet (ﷺ) while others among them disbelieve in him, just as people differ in their treatment of their parents. Ibn 'Asakir said: When Allah mentioned tawhid (affirmation of the Oneness of God) and steadfastness, He joined the command concerning parents to it, as it is paired with it in more than one verse of the Qur'an. Both of these views are unconvincing as an explanation of the connection.

In my view, the connection is that this passage shifts to another statement of the polytheists, namely their speech denying the Resurrection and their disputing about it, for that is among the fundamentals of their disbelief and the central concern here. Among these verses is His saying: ﴿And the one who says to his parents, "Uff to you both!"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17], up to His saying: ﴿losers﴾.

This is cast in the style of a story of a dispute between believing parents and a disbelieving child, and a story of a dispute between a believing child and disbelieving parents, because this style has an effect on the hearts of the listeners. It is also reported that this refers to a dispute that took place between 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr al-Siddiq, before his conversion to Islam, and his parents, as will come. Therefore, what precedes it must be a preparation and a introduction to mention of this dispute.

Al-Wahidi reported from Ibn 'Abbas that His saying ﴿And We have enjoined upon man (goodness) toward his parents﴾ up to His saying ﴿they are promised﴾ was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq. Ibn 'Atiyya and others said: It was revealed concerning Abu Bakr, his father Abu Quhafa, and his mother Umm al-Khayr, all of whom embraced Islam.

The command to honour parents is repeated in the Qur'an, and the Prophet (ﷺ) urged it on many occasions. Therefore, honouring one's parents is more manifest in this community than in others, and it is among the blessings of its people, to such a degree that honouring parents has not reached in any other nation the level it has reached among the Muslims.

The verse ﴿And We have enjoined upon man (goodness) toward his parents﴾ has already been mentioned in Surat al-'Ankabut [29:8].

By "man" (al-insan) is meant the species, that is, We enjoined people; and it is intended to refer specifically to those people to whom the Messengers came with the commands of Allah, and to those who believed and did righteous deeds. This is what fits His saying at its end: ﴿Those are the ones from whom We accept the best of what they did﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 16], and so on.

The same applies to the other verses on this theme, as in Surat al-'Ankabut and in Surat Luqman, in one and the same wording.

Al-husn (goodness) is a verbal noun from ḥasuna (to be good), meaning: We enjoined him to treat them with good conduct. This is how the majority (al-Jumhur) read it. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read it as iḥsānan. In both readings the accusative (nasb) is either by removal of the preposition, which is the bāʾ (with), or by implying in "wa-ṣṣaynā" (We enjoined) the meaning of "alzamnā" (We obligated).

Al-kurh, with a fatḥa or a ḍamma on the kāf, is a verbal noun from akraha, used when one is averse to something; that is, his carrying [the child] was disagreeable to him, meaning during its carrying and its birth.

The majority read kurhan in both places with a fatḥa on the kāf. ʿĀṣim, Ḥamza, al-Kisāʾī, Ibn Dhakwan on the authority of Ibn ʿĀmir, and Yaʿqub read it with a ḍamma on the kāf in both places. Kurhan is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), meaning: she was unwilling, or in a state of unwillingness.

The meaning is that she carried him in her womb, tired from carrying him, with a fatigue that made her averse to the conditions of that pregnancy.

She gave birth to him with pains and agonies that made her averse to his delivery. In that carrying and delivery there is a benefit for him, which is the benefit of his existence, the perfection of the state of a possible being, and what follows from his existence of faith and righteous deeds, through which the eternal blessings are attained.

What follows the carrying is pointed to, namely his nursing, by which his life is sustained and the pain of hunger is removed from him, and which is a hard labour for his mother. Therefore the period of carrying and nursing is mentioned, because its length requires the mother's patience in bearing the hardship of the foetus and the suckling.

Al-fiṣāl means weaning. Weaning is mentioned because it marks the end of the period of nursing. He mentioned the beginning of the period of carrying by "wa-ḥamluhu" (his carrying), and the end of nursing by "wa-fiṣāluhu" (his weaning). The meaning is: his carrying and his weaning together are thirty months.

Yaʿqub read wa-faṣluhu with a sukūn on the ṣād, meaning his separation from nursing, as indicated by the context.

Among the subtle meanings of the verse is that the period of carrying is combined with weaning into thirty months, so as to correspond to the various periods of carrying. For the carrying may be six months, seven months, eight months, or nine months, which is the most common. It has been said: When a woman's carrying was nine months, which is the most common, she nursed the child for twenty-one months; when the carrying was eight months, she nursed him for twenty-two months; when the carrying was seven months, she nursed him for twenty-three months; and when the carrying was six months, she nursed him for twenty-four months, which is the maximum period of nursing. Thus they compensated for the shortfall of each month of the period of carrying with an additional month of nursing, because the shortness of the period of carrying affects the child with weakness.

Among the subtle features of this compression in the verse is that it is capable of indicating that the period of carrying may be fewer than nine months. Were it not that it may be fewer than nine months, it would have fixed it at nine months, because the purpose is to establish the mother's right to honour on account of the hardship she bore in carrying, for the hardship of the period of carrying is greater than the hardship of nursing. Therefore, were it not intended to hint at this indication, fixing it at nine months would have been more fitting for the context.

ʿAlī ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) took this verse together with the verse in Surat al-Baqarah, ﴿And mothers suckle their children for two complete years﴾ [al-Baqarah: 233], as evidence that delivery may occur after six months. Something similar is attributed to Ibn ʿAbbas. They narrated from Maʿmar ibn ʿAbd Allah al-Juhani, who said: A man among us married a woman from Juhayna, and she gave birth at the completion of six months. Her husband went to ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan and informed him. ʿUthman sent for her, and when she was brought, he ordered her to be stoned. This reached ʿAli

﴿Until, when he reaches his full strength and reaches forty years, he says: "My Lord, enable me to be grateful for Your blessing with which You have blessed me and my parents, and to do righteousness that You approve, and make my offspring righteous for me. Indeed I have repented to You, and indeed I am of the Muslims."﴾

"Ḥattā" (until) here is initial (ibtidāʾiyya, introducing a new stage), and its meaning is that of the fāʾ of consequence (tafrīʿ) upon the preceding statement. Since "ḥattā" never loses the sense of a limit (ghāya, endpoint), it indicates here that the human being progressed through his stages from the time of his weaning until he reached his full strength (ashuddahu). That is, he is enjoined to honour his parents in the stages that follow his weaning: his guardian enjoins him during the stages of his childhood, and then it is incumbent upon him to observe the command of Allah at the time of his legal responsibility (taklīf).

The occurrence of "idhā" (when) after "ḥattā" serves to order upon it the specification of what comes after the limit from the report. That is, the limit was the time of his reaching his full strength. Similar instances of this have come up earlier, near and far from here, such as His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿until, when you lost courage﴾ [Āl ʿImrān: 152] in Surat Āl ʿImrān.

Since "idhā" is an adverb of future time, the past-tense verb after it is turned into the future. It is expressed in the past form only to present the thing whose attainment is certain as if it had already happened; so it is a metaphor (istiʿāra).

And "idhā" here is a stripping away (tajrīd) of the metaphor. The meaning is: until he reaches his full strength, that is, he continues in goodness toward them until he reaches his full strength; then, when he reaches it, ﴿he says: "My Lord, enable me"﴾, that is, he asks Allah for help to increase his goodness toward them, by being inspired to give thanks for His blessings upon him and upon his parents.

Among the blessings upon him is that He inspired him to do good to his parents.

Among the blessings upon his parents is that He made this child serve them, so that he would do good to them. These two blessings are the first that come to mind from the general blessing of Allah upon him and upon his parents, because the context is about the two of them.

This is an indication that the act tied to the time of reaching full strength, which is the act of ﴿he says: "My Lord, enable me"﴾, is part of what the human being was enjoined. That is, he should do good to his parents at the time of reaching full strength. So the meaning is: And We enjoined upon man goodness toward his parents, even in the time of his reaching full strength; that is, he should not slacken in doing good to them in every way, even by supplicating for them.

He specified the time of reaching full strength because it is a time when a great deal of effort is required in seeking sustenance, since he then has a wife and children, and the burdens of a woman increase, so that he has a husband, a household and children. These are likely to distract them from attending to their parents and doing good to them. So he is alerted that they should not slacken in doing good to their parents.

The meaning of ﴿he says: "My Lord, enable me"﴾ is that he supplicated his Lord with that. Its meaning is that he is commanded to call [others] to good for them, in that his supplication for himself does not distract him from supplicating for them, and that he does good to them in their absence when he is privately conversing with his Lord. Therefore, his doing good to them in their presence is certainly achieved by the implication of the address, as in the method of implication (fahwā al-khiṭāb) in the prohibition of harming them by His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿So do not say to them "Uff"﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 23].

The summary of the meaning is that Allah commanded goodness to parents both in their presence and in their absence, and by every means of goodness whose ultimate purpose is that they benefit, and this is the meaning of His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And say: "My Lord, have mercy upon them as they raised me when I was small"﴾ [al-Isrāʾ: 24]. And when Allah commanded supplication for both parents, He promised to answer it through His Messenger (ﷺ), in accordance with his saying: "When the son of Adam dies, his deeds come to an end except for three: ongoing charity, knowledge that benefits people, and a righteous child who prays for him."

The son's thanking his Lord for the blessing that Allah bestowed upon his parents is nothing but a form of acting on their behalf in this thanks, and it is among the deeds that the child performs on behalf of his parents.

In the hadith of al-Fadl ibn ʿAbbas: that a woman of Khath'am said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on the day of the Farewell Pilgrimage: "Indeed the obligation of Allah upon His servants regarding the Hajj has reached my father, an aged old man who cannot sit steady on his mount. Will it suffice if I perform the Hajj on his behalf?" He said: "Yes, perform the Hajj on his behalf." This was a Hajj that was not obligatory upon her father because of his incapacity.
