Al-ashudd (full strength) is the state of the mental and physical faculties reaching their vigour. It is a plural for which no singular form has been heard. It has been said its singular is shidda, with a kasra on the shīn and the feminine tāʾ, like niʿma whose plural is anʿum. Al-ashudd is not the name of a fixed number of years of life; rather, years of life are only the approximate period in which full strength occurs. Its time is after thirty years, and its completion is at forty years. For this reason, His saying ﴿and reached forty years﴾ is coordinated after ﴿reached his full strength﴾, meaning: he reached full strength and attained its perfection. This is like His saying (Exalted is He): ﴿And when he reached his full strength and became perfect﴾ [al-Qasas: 14], which was mentioned in Surat Yusuf. And His saying ﴿and reached forty years﴾ is not an emphatic restatement of ﴿reached his full strength﴾, because repeating the verb "reached" distances the possibility of emphasis, and the particle of coordination also distances that possibility.

And "awzi'nī" (enable me) means: inspire me. The original sense of the verb awza'a is the removal of restraint (wazaʿ), that is, withholding from some action; so the hamza in it indicates removal. It was mentioned earlier in Surat al-Naml.

"Niʿmatak" (Your blessing) is a verbal noun (ism al-maṣdar) in construct form which is general in scope, meaning: inspire me to thank for the blessings with which You have blessed me and my parents, from all religious blessings such as faith and success, and from worldly blessings such as health and wealth.

[Page 34]

The supplication for his offspring mentioned in his words ﴿And set right for me my offspring﴾ is a digression (*istitrad*) within the injunction to supplicate for one's parents. The point is that a person should not neglect to think about his own future, and should direct his care toward his offspring just as he directed it toward his parents, so that he may receive from his children's kindness to him the like of what he showed to his parents. Setting right one's offspring includes inspiring them to supplicate for their father.

Incorporating the instruction to supplicate for the setting right of his offspring into a passage whose context is kindness to parents hints that a man will receive from his children's kindness to him the like of what his parents received from his kindness to them. It also hints that a father's supplication for his son is hoped to be answered. In the hadith of Abu Hurayra on the authority of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Three supplications are answered, with no doubt about them: the supplication of a parent against his child, the supplication of a traveler, and the supplication of one who has been wronged." In another narration it reads "for his child." It is a *hasan* (good) hadith with multiple chains of transmission.

The *lam* in ﴿And set right for me﴾ is the *lam* of cause (*lam al-'illa*), meaning: set right my offspring for my sake and for my benefit, as in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh: 1]. The reason for adding this in the supplication is that, after he had mentioned God's blessings upon him and upon his parents, he turned to the gifts of God and asked Him to set right his offspring, and he indicated that their being set right was for his own benefit. This is a preparation for the spreading out of the answer, as if he were saying: just as You began with me by Your blessing, and began with my parents by Your blessing, and granted them enjoyment through my being guided to show them kindness, complete Your favor by setting right my offspring, for their being set right is for my good. These are wonderful ascents through the degrees of closeness.

The meaning of the locative sense in ﴿in my offspring﴾ is that his offspring are treated as a container (*zarf*) in which what constitutes the setting right settles and which encloses it. This indicates that the setting right takes firm hold of the offspring and penetrates them. A parallel usage of this locative sense is His words, exalted is He, ﴿And He made it a word that remains in his descendants﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 28].

The clause ﴿Indeed I have repented to You﴾ serves as a justification for the request made in the supplication, a justification by way of seeking means (*tawassul*) through the bond of faith and through acknowledging the blessing and servitude.

The particle *inna* (إنَّ) here serves to emphasize the predicate, as is clear. In this way the particle *inna* is used in a context of causal justification and takes the place of the *fa* (فاء) of consequence.

The intended meaning of "repentance" (*tawba*) is faith, because it is a turning away from polytheism. By "being among the Muslims" is meant that he followed the laws of Islam, which are the deeds. He said "among the Muslims" rather than "and I have submitted," as he said "I have repented to You," because of what the active participle (*ism al-fa'il*) indicates of being characterized by an action in the present, which is renewal, since deeds are renewed and repeated. Faith, however, is attained at once and so is settled, since it is a conviction. In addition, there is the observance of the verse-ending (*fasila*). This is the way of interpreting the verse according to what its structures and arrangement indicate, without strain or forcing. It is general for every Muslim who is fit to be entrusted with God's injunction concerning his parents and to supplicate for them, if they are believers.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 46, verse 16:

﴿Those are the ones from whom the best of what they did is accepted, and over whose evil deeds is overlooked, among the companions of Paradise; a true promise which they were promised.﴾

The demonstrative (ism al-isharah) has been used for the purpose we mentioned a moment ago, at His words ﴿Those are the companions of Paradise, abiding therein﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 14]. That it is a demonstrative of the plural, and that the pronouns referring back to it are plural, is evident in that the intended meaning of "man" in His words ﴿And We have enjoined upon man﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 15] is not a specific individual, but rather the genus (al-jins) used in the sense of comprehensiveness (al-istighraq), as we have previously explained.

The sentence is a resumptive sentence of explanatory type (istinaf bayani), because what precedes it, of description and exhortation, produces in the listener an expectation to know the benefit of that; so His words (﴿Those are the ones from whom We accept﴾) to the end are an answer to that elevation of expectation.

The generality of "the best of what they did" gives the sentence the benefit of a concluding summary (tadhyil), meaning: goodness toward the two parents, and supplication for them and for the offspring, is among the best of deeds, so it is among the best of what they did. And all that is accepted from them is the best of what they did. Acceptance (al-taqabbul) is the consequence of deeds' effects, such as reward for deeds and the answering of supplication. In this there is an indication that this supplication is hoped to be answered, because God Himself took charge of teaching it, like the supplication in Surat al-Fatiha and the supplication at the end of Surat al-Baqarah.

The verb "yutaqabbalu" is construed with the particle (ʿan), whereas its proper construction would be with (min), giving precedence to the side of those for whom supplication is made, namely the parents and the offspring; because the child's and the parent's supplication for those people is in the position of acting on their behalf in the worship of supplication. And when action performed on someone's behalf is accepted, it is known that a person's action for himself is also accepted. So there is an ellipsis in the speech, as if it were said: "Those, from them is accepted, and on behalf of their parents and offspring is accepted, the best of what they did."

The Jumhur read "yutaqabbalu" and "yutajawazu" with a yā' (ya) that is vowelled with a ḍammah, both in the passive voice (mabniyyān lil-nāʾib), and "aḥsanu" is nominative as a substitute for the subject (nāʾib ʿan al-fāʿil); the subject is not mentioned because it is evident that the one who accepts is God. Ḥamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, and Khalaf read both with two fatḥah-vowelled nūns and "aḥsana" in the accusative.

His words "﴿among the companions of Paradise﴾" are in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relative to the demonstrative, meaning: being among the companions of Paradise, at the time when the best of what they did is accepted and over whose evil deeds is overlooked, because the companions of Paradise have their best deeds accepted and their evil deeds overlooked. This is mentioned to honour them, that they are of the esteemed group, as one says: "He honours him among the people of knowledge."

﴿A true promise﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the acceptance and overlooking implied by "yutaqabbalu" and "yutajawazu"; so the circumstantial element came from the verbal noun implied by the verb, just as the pronoun was repeated in His words, exalted is He, ﴿Be just; that is nearer to piety﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 8], meaning: justice is nearer to piety.

The word "wa'd" (promise) is a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle (maf'ul), meaning: that is their promised destination which they were promised.

The genitive construction "wa'd" with "al-sidq" is a construction in the sense of "min" (of), meaning: a promise from truth, since it does not fail.

And ﴿which they were promised﴾ is an attribute of "a true promise," meaning: that is what they were promised in this world through the Qur'an, in the verses urging kindness to the two parents, gratitude, and the setting right of the offspring.

[Page 37]

This group is the subject of these verses, which begin with His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have enjoined upon man﴾ (Al-Ahqaf 46:15). This is the group that disbelieved in its Lord and mistreated its parents. It is known that the parents were believers, from His saying (﴿Do you promise me that I will be brought forth, when generations have passed before me?﴾) and the rest of the verse.

The better view is that the phrase ﴿And the one who says to his parents﴾ is coordinated with the phrase ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, clear proofs﴾ (Al-Ahqaf 46:7) and what follows it. It is a transition to another of the roots of their polytheism, namely the denial of resurrection.

As for His saying ﴿And the one who says to his parents﴾, the sound approach is to treat it as an object of an implied verb, whose sense is: "Remember the one who said to his parents," because this reading suits all the possibilities.

It may also be taken as a subject (mubtada'), with the phrase ﴿Those are the ones against whom the Word has come into effect, among nations﴾ (Al-Ahqaf 46:18) as its predicate, according to one of the two possibilities regarding the referent of the demonstrative in His saying ﴿Those are the ones against whom the Word has come into effect﴾ (Al-Ahqaf 46:18).

The word "alladhi" (the one who) here is a noun that applies to the group characterized by its relative clause. This describes a category of the children of the polytheists whose fathers had embraced Islam and called them to Islam, but they did not respond to them and spoke harshly to them. To their disbelief they added the abominable sin of disobedience to parents, which is ugly because it contradicts the innate nature (fitrah) upon which Allah created people, since the condition of parents with their children requires that they be treated with kindness. This is also indicated by the fact that the statement at its end, ﴿Those are the ones against whom the Word has come into effect﴾ (Al-Ahqaf 46:18), to the end of the verse, is not restricted to a specific person.

The view held by the majority of commentators (mufassirun) is that the verse does not refer to a specific individual, and that what is meant by it is a group whose fathers embraced Islam while they themselves did not become Muslims at that time.

It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, Marwan ibn al-Hakam, Mujahid, al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj that it was revealed concerning a son of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, whose name was 'Abd al-Ka'bah, whom the Prophet (ﷺ) named 'Abd al-Rahman after he embraced Islam. They said: He was a polytheist before the Hijrah, and his father Abu Bakr and his mother Umm Ruman used to call him to Islam and remind him of resurrection, and he would respond to them with words like those mentioned in this verse. He would say: "Where are Abdullah ibn Jud'an, and Uthman ibn Amr, and Amir ibn Ka'b, and the elders of Quraysh, so that I may ask them about what Muhammad says?" However, the verse is not specific to him, such that it would be revealed concerning him. In this light is to be understood the statement of 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, when Marwan ibn al-Hakam said to 'Abd al-Rahman: "He is the one about whom Allah says: ﴿And the one who says to his parents: Uff to you both!﴾." This was in the context of 'Abd al-Rahman's suggestion to Marwan, when Marwan was taking the pledge of allegiance for Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah by making him heir apparent to the caliphate.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, in the Book of Tafsir, it is reported from Yusuf ibn Mahak that he said: Marwan ibn al-Hakam was the governor of the Hijaz, appointed by Mu'awiyah. He gave a sermon and began to mention Yazid ibn Mu'awiyah, so that the people would pledge allegiance to him after his father. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr said to him: "Is it Heraclian?" meaning: "Have you made it an inheritance, like the rule of Heraclius?" Marwan said: "Seize him!" He entered the house of 'A'ishah, and they could not reach him. Marwan said: "This is the one about whom Allah revealed: ﴿And the one who says to his parents: Uff to you both!﴾." 'A'ishah said from behind the curtain: "Allah did not reveal anything concerning us in the Qur'an, except that Allah revealed my innocence (i.e., my exoneration)." How then could what is meant by ﴿And the one who says to his parents: Uff to you both!﴾ be 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr, when the end of the verse says ﴿Those are the ones against whom the Word has come into effect﴾ (Al-Ahqaf 46:18), to the word "losers"? It uses the demonstrative for the plural and passes judgment on those spoken of as being lost. I have not found anyone who was a polytheist while his parents were believers. Whatever the case, 'Abd al-Rahman embraced Islam before the Conquest, and when he embraced Islam, his Islam erased what came before it, and he was excluded from the threat in His saying ﴿Those are the ones against whom the Word has come into effect﴾ (Al-Ahqaf 46:18) and what follows, because that is a threat, and every threat is conditional in its fulfilment upon the one threatened dying without being a believer. This is known necessarily from the Shari'ah. This is called, among the Ash'arites (al-Ash'ariyyah, followers of the theological school of Abu al-Hasan al-Ash'ari), the question of "muwafah" (the ending of one's life in faith or unbelief). Moreover, it has been said that the demonstrative in His saying "Those" refers back to "the former ones" in His saying ﴿This is nothing but the myths of the former peoples﴾ (Al-Ahqaf 46:17), as will come.

"Uff" (أُفٍّ) is a verb-like word (ism fi'l) meaning: "I am annoyed." Its discussion has already passed in Surah Al-Isra and in Surah Al-Anbiya. Here it is used metaphorically to denote the least harm, so those who harm their parents with more than this are deeper in the abominable disobedience and more deserving of the judgment, by the indication of the implied meaning of the address (dalalat fahwa al-khitab), as established in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So do not say to them, "Uff"﴾ (Al-Isra 17:23) in Surah Al-Isra.

Nafi' and Hafs from 'Asim read "uffin" with a kasra on the fa' and with tanwin. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Ya'qub read "uffa" with a fatha on the fa' without tanwin. The rest read "uffi" with a kasra on the fa' without tanwin. These are three dialectal forms of this word.

Know that in His saying ﴿And the one who says to his parents: Uff to you both!﴾ there is an aesthetic of metrical balance (muhassin al-ittizan), for it is in the meter of a hemistich of al-ramal (a poetic meter), whose 'arud (final foot of the first hemistich) is shortened (mahdhufah) and whose darb (final foot of the second hemistich) is shortened. It contains khabn (dropping of the second letter of a foot) and qabd (dropping of the fifth letter of a foot), and kaff (dropping of the seventh letter of a foot) is added to it according to the reading of those other than Nafi' and Hafs.

The interrogative in ﴿Do you promise me that I will be brought forth﴾ is a rejection and an expression of astonishment. "Ikhraj" (being brought forth) means resurrection after death.

The clause of circumstance, ﴿when generations have passed before me﴾, is made a qualifier of the extremity of the rejection, meaning: How can that be, when generations have passed?

"Qurun" (generations) is the plural of "qarn," which is a community whose lifetimes are close to one another. In a hadith: "The best of generations is my generation, then those who come after them," and Exalted is He said: ﴿Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations who were stronger than him and greater in number?﴾ (Al-Qasas 28:78).

The meaning is that he deemed it impossible that he himself should be brought out of the earth after death, when many nations have passed and much time has elapsed over them without any of them coming out. This is either a misunderstanding of the meaning of resurrection or a sophistry in argumentation, because the promise of resurrection was not fixed to a specific time, nor was it stated that it would occur in this world.

[Page 39]

The majority read "Ata'iddanni" with two separate nuns, while Hisham, from Ibn 'Amir, read it with the two nuns assimilated (idgham).

The meaning of ﴿they both seek help from Allah﴾ is that they ask Allah for help, that is, they ask Allah to guide him. So the meaning is: they both seek Allah's help on his behalf.

The clause ﴿Woe to you! Believe﴾ is not an explanation of the meaning of their seeking help. Rather, it is the speech (maqul) of an implied saying, indicated by the meaning of the clause.

The word ﴿woe﴾ (waylaka) is a word of threat and intimidation.

"Wayl" means evil. The original form of "waylaka" is "waylun laka," as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands﴾ (Al-Baqarah 2:79). When its usage became frequent and they wanted to shorten it, they dropped the lam and attached the second-person pronoun to the word "wayl," putting it in the accusative by dropping the preposition.

The verb "amin" (believe) is treated as intransitive, meaning: characterize yourself with faith, which is the call of Islam. The clause ﴿Indeed, the promise of Allah is true﴾ is a reason for the command to believe, and an implicit warning that the promise of Allah may become binding upon him.

"Asatir" is the plural of "usturah," which means a story. Its use has come to be applied to a false or fabricated story, just as one says "khurafah" (fable). It has already been discussed in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when it is said to them, "What has your Lord revealed?" they say, "Myths of the former peoples"﴾ (Al-Nahl 16:24) in Surah Al-Nahl, and in His saying ﴿And they say, "Myths of the former peoples, which he has had written down"﴾ (Al-Furqan 25:5) in Surah Al-Furqan.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 46, verse 18:

﴿Those are the ones against whom the word has been justified, among nations that passed away before them of jinn and mankind. Indeed, they were losers.﴾

It is permissible that the demonstrative noun (ism al-isharah) refers back to the one who said this statement (al-ladhi qala ladayhi hadhihi al-maqalah), since you know that the intended meaning is a group (fariq). The indication therefore came with the demonstrative of the plural, by interpreting it as a group (ta'wil al-fariq).

Page 40
It is also permissible that "ulaika" (those) is an indication to "al-awwalin" (the earlier ones) from His saying ﴿Then he says, "This is nothing but the myths of the earlier people."﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17]. They are the ones concerning whom it is narrated that the son of Abu Bakr mentioned them when he said: "Where is 'Abd Allah ibn Jud'an, and where is 'Uthman ibn 'Amr, and the elders of Quraysh," as has been mentioned just before. Summoning this group by means of the demonstrative noun serves to further distinguish their astonishing condition.

The definiteness of "al-qawl" (the word) is the definiteness of previous reference (ta'rif al-'ahd), and it is a statement well known among the Muslims, because the Qur'an repeatedly expresses it as "al-qawl" in such verses as ﴿He said, "So the truth, and the truth I say"﴾ [Sad: 84] ﴿"I will surely fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you of them, all together."﴾ [Sad: 85], and like His saying ﴿Then is one upon whom the word of punishment has been justified...﴾ [al-Zumar: 19], for the "kalimah" is a "qawl", and like His saying ﴿Certainly the word has come into effect upon most of them, so they do not believe﴾ [Ya-Sin: 7], and the verse.

Its unrestricted use in this verse is elegant for its suitability. . . .

The insertion of ﴿kanu khasirin﴾ (they were losers) without saying "innahum khasirun" (indeed they are losers) is to indicate that their loss is certain, so it is expressed metaphorically by making them as those who exist within it.

The emphasis of the statement with the particle (inna) is because they think that what they obtained in this world of enjoying good things is a success after which there is no distress, because they do not believe in the resurrection and recompense. Thus the state of their thinking is compared to the state of a merchant whose profit from his trade is small, so that his affair becomes a loss. Among its previous occurrences more than once is His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿So their trade did not profit﴾ [al-Baqarah: 16] in al-Baqarah.

The mention of the verb of being (kana) in His saying ﴿kanu khasirin﴾ rather than limiting it to "khasirin" is because (kana) indicates that the loss is firmly established upon them.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 46, verse 19:

﴿And for each are ranks according to what they did, and that He may fully repay them their deeds, and they will not be wronged.﴾

It is a conjunction (ʿatf) with the preceding discourse, from His saying ﴿Those are the ones upon whom the word has come into effect﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 18], then His saying ﴿Those are the ones upon whom the word has come into effect﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 18], and so on.

The tanwin on "kull" (kullin) is the tanwin of compensation (ʿiwad) for that to which kull is attached, and that is omitted but understood from the context. That is, "and for each of the two groups: the believer who is dutiful to his parents, and the disbeliever who combines disbelief and disobedience to parents."

Darajat ("ranks"), that is, gradations of difference in the reward for the people of good recompense, who are the believers, and degrees (darakat) in evil for the people of disbelief.

The expression of those gradations as "darajat" is a case of taghlib (predominance of one term over the other), because the daraja is a rank in elevation, and that elevation is figurative; it suits only the ranks of good. As for the lowest rank, it is the darakah, as He - exalted is He - said: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites will be in the lowest depth of the Fire﴾ [an-Nisa: 145].

The purpose of this emphasis is to highlight the status of the people of good.

The "min" in His saying "mimma ʿamilu" ("according to what they did") is partitive (tabʿidiyyah). The intended meaning of "ma ʿamilu" is the recompense for what they did, so a noun is to be supplied (the recompense of). The "darajat" are the ranks of deeds in good and its opposite, by which the recompense is according to their measure.

It is also possible that "min" is inceptive (ibtidaiyyah), and "ma ʿamilu" is the deed itself, so no noun is supplied, and "darajat" are the ranks of recompense which correspond to the deeds. The measures of that are known only to God, and they vary by quantity, by precedence, and by distinction. So the one who said to his parents "Uff to you both" and denied the resurrection, then later embraced Islam, may be of a lesser rank than the one who hastened to Islam and to dutifulness to his parents and the righteous deeds that follow his Islam. All of this is according to the ranks.

He indicated that the recompense for all those ranks is according to a measure known to God. His saying after it, "and that He may fully repay them their deeds," is the cause (ʿillah) of an omitted element indicated by the discourse, and its estimate is: We decreed their recompense according to the measures of their ranks, that He may fully repay them the recompense of their deeds; that is, We reward them completely and fully, without any deficiency in it.

The majority read "wa-linuwaffiyahum" with the nun of majesty (nun al-ʿazamah). Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, ʿAsim, Hisham from Ibn ʿAmir, and Yaʿqub read it with the yaʾ (third person), referring it back to God - exalted is He - since that is known from the context.

The clause ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ is a precautionary qualification (ihtiras), with regard to the fulfilment for one of the two groups, namely the group deserving punishment, lest it be supposed that the fulfilment regarding them means that the recompense be harsher than what their deeds require.

[Page 42]

﴿On the Day when those who disbelieved are exposed to the Fire: "You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them. So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation, for what you used to be arrogant about on earth without right, and for what you used to commit corruption."﴾ This is a transition to the threat against the disbelievers for disbelief in its entirety, and that is in addition to the earlier threat, which concerned their denial of the Resurrection together with their disobedience to their two Muslim parents.

The sentence is therefore conjoined (ma'tuf) to the sentence "And the one who said to his parents, 'Uff to you both!'" and the verses that follow it.

The discourse is a quoted speech (maqul qawl) of a deleted verb of saying, whose estimated form is: "And it will be said to those who disbelieved on the Day they are exposed to the Fire: 'You squandered your good things.'" The reason for mentioning it here is that it confirms the meaning of "they will not be wronged" (la yuzlamun), that is, they will not be wronged in the recompense of the Hereafter, even though We bestowed favours upon them in this world. Had We wished, We could have hastened their recompense for their disbelief in the worldly life, but Allah did not deprive them of blessing in the worldly life. The blessing of the disbeliever in this world is indeed a blessing according to the verifying theologians (al-muhaqqiqin min al-mutakallimin, the mutakallimun being the scholars of kalam, or speculative theology). It is related from al-Ash'ari that the disbeliever is not favoured in this world, but this has been interpreted as a verbal disagreement, meaning that it is considered from the standpoint that its outcome is evil. The blessing of Allah in this world is a dealing governed by the bounty of lordship (fadl al-rububiyya), while their recompense for their deeds in the Hereafter is a dealing governed by the justice of divinity (adl al-ilahiyya) and wisdom.

The phrase "on the Day He is exposed" (yawma yu'radu) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarfiyya) governed by the deleted verb of saying.

The word "exposure" (al-'ardh) has been discussed in His words "Those are exposed to their Lord" in Surat Hud, in His words "The Fire, to which they are exposed" in Surat Ghafir, and in His words "And you will see them exposed to it" in Surat al-Shura.

The phrase "squandering the good things" (idhhab al-tayyibat) is a metaphor for their departure from them, just as the removal of a person (idhhab al-mar') is his distancing from his place. Dhahab means to depart.

The meaning is: you have exhausted what was yours of good things through what came to you of the blessings and pleasures of this world, so no good things remain for you after them, because you did not work to attain the good things of the Hereafter. This is a warning (i'dhar) to them and a confirmation that they will not be wronged. Accordingly, His words "So today you will be recompensed with the punishment of humiliation" follow from it.

The fa' here is an eloquent fa' (fa' fasiha), which implies a condition. The estimated sense is: "If it is so, then today nothing remains for you except the recompense of your evil deeds"

[Page 43]

. The fa' is not for sequential arrangement (tafriq) nor for causation (tasabbub). There is nothing in the verse that requires preventing the Muslim from enjoying good things in this world, provided he seeks what is lawful of them and performs his religious duties, with regard to everything beyond that. Although abstention from concern for such things is of higher rank, which is the rank of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and of some of his Companions.

Al-Hasan related from al-Ahnaf ibn Qays that he heard 'Umar ibn al-Khattab say: "I know best about the ease of living, and had I wished, I could have made for myself livers, delicacies, and [foods]..., and humps, but I saw that Allah censured a people when He said: 'You squandered your good things in your worldly life and enjoyed them.'" 'Umar intended by this only fear lest that should preoccupy him from his duty of managing the affairs of the community, so that he would fall into negligence and be held accountable for it.

Ibn 'Atiyya mentioned that when 'Umar entered Syria, Khalid ibn al-Walid brought to him a good food. 'Umar said: "This is for us; what then of the poor Muslims who died without being satisfied with barley bread?" Khalid said: "For them is Paradise." Then 'Umar wept and said: "If our portion is in this world and they have gone with Paradise, then they have indeed left us far behind."

Al-Hawn means humiliation (al-hawan), which is abasement (al-dhull). The annexation of "punishment" (adhab) to "humiliation" (al-hawn) is an annexation of the qualified to its qualifier (idafat al-mawsuf ila al-sifa).

The bi' in His words "for what you used to be arrogant about" is causal (sababiyya), and it is connected to the verb "you will be recompensed" (tujzawna).

By arrogance (al-istikbar) is meant arrogance toward the Messenger (ﷺ) and toward accepting monotheism.

Corruption (al-fusuq) is departure from the religion and from the truth. A Muslim may partake of a share of these two offences, and so he will have a share of their recompense which the disbelievers encounter, and that is explained in the rulings of the religion.

Corruption here means polytheism (al-shirk).

[Page 44]

The majority of reciters (al-jumhur) read "adhhabtum" with one hamza, as a declarative statement used in the sense of rebuke (tawbikh).

Ibn Kathir read "a-adhhabtum" with two hamzas, as a rebuking interrogative.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 46, verse 21:

﴿Remember the brother of 'Ad, when he warned his people in al-Ahqaf, and warners had already passed before him and after him, saying: Worship none but God. I fear for you the punishment of a tremendous day.﴾

The story of Hud and his people is told in the manner of an admonition to the polytheists who denied the Qur'an, as God related about them from the beginning of this surah in His words: ﴿And those who disbelieve turn away from what they are warned of﴾ (46:3). It is joined to the proofs that preceded it, from His words ﴿Say: Have you considered what you call upon besides God?﴾ (46:4), which is matched by Hud's words ﴿that you worship none but God﴾, and then His words ﴿Say: I am not a novelty among the messengers﴾ (46:9), which is matched by His words ﴿and warners had already passed before him and after him.﴾ All of this is an admonition through the condition of Hud with his people. The story is also told as proof for the mission of Muhammad ﷺ and against the obstinacy of his people, by mentioning an example of their condition with their messenger through the condition of 'Ad with their messenger. It also serves to console the Messenger ﷺ for the obstinacy and slander his people met him with, so that it is both an admonition and a consolation, each of which takes from it what suits him.

You will not find a word that unites both meanings better than the word "remember" (udhkur), because it fits the meaning of verbal mention (dhikr al-lisani), that he is to say this to his people, and the meaning of remembrance (dhukr, with a dammah), that he recalls that condition in his own soul, even if it had already happened to him and to others like him, because in recollection there is consolation and an example. This is like His words, exalted is He: ﴿Be patient over what they say, and remember Our servant David, the possessor of strength﴾ (38:17) in the surah of Sad.

Both meanings look back to His words just before: ﴿Say: I am not a novelty among the messengers﴾, for when he says this to them, they recall what they know of the stories of the messengers which the Qur'an has related to them before, and he himself recalls, without doubt, the conditions of many messengers. Then the story of Hud came as an example of that.

The polytheists of Mecca, when they recall their own condition and the condition of 'Ad, find the two conditions alike, so it is fitting for them to fear that what befell them may befall them too.

The restriction to mentioning 'Ad is because they were the first of the Arab nations to whom a messenger came after the general mission of Noah. The mission of Hud and the mission of Salih came before the mission of Abraham, peace be upon them all. After the mention of their story comes a general allusion to other Arab nations who denied the messengers, in His words, exalted is He: ﴿And We destroyed the towns around you﴾ (46:27), and so on.

The brother of 'Ad is Hud, and his biography has already been given in surah al-A'raf.

He is described here by his attribute rather than by his proper name, because the purpose of the mention here is the mention of an illustration and admonition to the Quraysh, that they are like 'Ad in turning away from the call of a messenger from among their own people.

"Brother" (akh) may refer to one who shares in the lineage of a tribe; they say: "O brother of the Banu so-and-so" and "O brother of the Arabs." This is what is meant here. It may also refer to one who is attached to or a companion of someone; it is said: "brother of war" and "brother of resolute deeds." The Prophet ﷺ said to Zayd ibn Harithah: "You are our brother and our client (mawla)." This is the meaning in His words, exalted is He: ﴿The people of Lot denied the messengers﴾ (26:160), ﴿When their brother Lot said to them: Will you not fear God?﴾ (26:161). Lot was not of the lineage of his people, the people of Sodom.

"When" (idh) is a noun denoting past time, and here it is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for "brother of 'Ad," meaning: remember the time of his warning to his people. So it is a badal al-ishtimal (a substitution of inclusion, where the second term is included within the first in a broader sense, rather than being identical with it).

The mention of warning here, rather than calling or sending, is because of the correspondence between the depiction of the condition of Hud's people and the condition of the people of Muhammad ﷺ. Al-Ahqaf is the plural of hiqf (with a kasrah and then a sukun), which is a great, elongated sand dune. These lands called al-Ahqaf were the dwellings of 'Ad, and they overlooked the sea between Oman and Aden. At the far end of al-Ahqaf is the land of Hadramawt. The mention of 'Ad was already made at His words, exalted is He: ﴿And to 'Ad their brother Hud﴾ (7:65) in surah al-A'raf.

The clause ﴿and warners had already passed before him and after him﴾ is a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah) between the clause "warned" and the clause ﴿that you worship none but God﴾, which explains it.

The clause "warned" has been explained by the clause ﴿that you worship none but God﴾, etc.

The "an" here is explanatory (tafsiriyyah), because "warned" contains the sense of saying without its letters.

The meaning of ﴿had already passed﴾ is "had gone before": that is, the warnings of other messengers. "Nudhur" is the plural of nidharah, with a kasrah on the nun.

The day is described as tremendous because of the great events that occur in it, so the description is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli).

This is a reply to His saying ﴿that you worship none but Allah﴾ [Hud: 26], and for this reason the verb "qalu" (they said) came disconnected (fasl), following the manner of dialogue.

The interrogative is a denial (inkar). The "coming" (majī') is used metaphorically for the intention of seeking a great matter: the arrival of the call after he had not been calling with it is likened to a coming that came to that place.

Al-Afk, with a fatha on the hamza, means turning away (al-sarf), and they intended by it the meaning of abandonment (al-tark), i.e., "that we abandon the worship of our gods."

This denial is an allusion to accusation of lying (ta'ridh bi'l-takdhib), and therefore the statement ﴿Then bring us what you threaten us with, if you are among the truthful﴾ follows it as a consequence, so they openly declared his lying by way of implication (mafhum).

Page 47
The meaning is: "Bring us the punishment with which you threaten us," namely the punishment of the great Day. They turned the intended meaning of Hud regarding the punishment to the specific punishment of this world, because they did not believe in the Resurrection, and his saying after it ﴿So when they saw it as a cloud approaching﴾ and His saying ﴿Rather, it is what you were hasting for﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 24] indicate this. They meant: "Bring it to us now," because the context is one of denial, with the claim that worshipping their gods would bring them punishment.

And "min al-sadiqin" (among the truthful) is more emphatic in describing truthfulness than saying "in kunta sadiqan" (if you are truthful), as has been established in His saying, exalted is He, ﴿and was among the disbelievers﴾ in Surat al-Baqarah, i.e., "if you are, in this statement of yours, among those who were truthful," meaning: if you do not bring it, then you are not truthful in it.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 46, verse 23:

﴿He said: "The knowledge is only with God; and I convey to you what I have been sent with. But I see you to be a people who are ignorant."﴾ When they made their statement, "So bring us what you threaten us with, if you are of the truthful," a separation between them and him concerning what he warned them of, namely that the worship of other than God necessitates the punishment of a great day, the matter in their saying "so bring it" implied immediacy, that is, they sought its hastening, so that it would show his truthfulness, since the norm is that one does not delay in manifesting his truthfulness to them.

The attribution of the "bringing" of the punishment to him is metaphorical (majaz), because he is the intermediary in the bringing of the punishment, by his supplicating God to hasten it; or they made the punishment something within his capacity, that he could bring whenever he wished, mocking him, since he had told them that he was sent from God. They made this imply that between him and God there is cooperation and obedience, that is, "do not delay in bringing it."

This implication is also indicated by his saying to them, when the punishment descended, ﴿Nay, it is what you were hastening for﴾. Therefore his reply was that he said, ﴿The knowledge is only with God﴾, that is, the knowledge of the time of the punishment's coming is kept with God; no one is informed of it. So the definite article in "al-'ilm" (the knowledge) is for generalization by convention (al-istighraq al-'urfi), that is, the knowledge of the unseen, or the definite article is a substitute for the genitive complement, that is, the time of the punishment. This reply applies to all the possibilities in the meaning of their saying "so bring us what you threaten us with," because all of them imply that he knows its time.

The restriction here is real, like His saying ﴿None but He will manifest it at its time﴾, and the purpose of this restriction is its inclusion of negating knowledge of the time of the punishment from the speaker, as a rebuttal to their saying "so bring us what you threaten us with."

And "with" (ʿinda) here is metaphorical for exclusivity in knowledge, that is, God alone is the knower of the time at which He sends the punishment, for a wisdom in its delay.

The meaning of ﴿and I convey to you what I have been sent with﴾ is that he was sent as a conveyer of God's command and His warning, and he was not sent to inform them of the time when the punishment would arrive, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿They ask you about the Hour: when is its appointed time? In what are you of mention of it? To your Lord is its finality. You are only a warner to those who fear it﴾. So His saying ﴿and I convey to you what I have been sent with﴾ is a parenthetical clause between the clause "the knowledge is only with God" and the clause "but I see you to be a people who are ignorant."

The place of the contrastive particle in His saying ﴿but I see you to be a people who are ignorant﴾ is that it is in contrast to His saying "the knowledge is only with God," that is, "but you are ignorant of God's attributes and the wisdom of His sending the messengers, so you suppose that the messengers are intermediaries for relaying the creation's demands to God, that He show them wonders and compete with them in desires." So the pivot of the contrast is the object of the predicate of "but" (lakinna), which is "a people who are ignorant," and the estimate is: "but you are a people who are ignorant." The placing of the contrastive particle upon the pronoun of the speaker is a deviation from the apparent form, so that he would not preempt them with the charge of ignorance, in order to draw down their fledgling (i.e., to soften their stance), so he made their ignorance something he merely suspected of them, that they might examine the soundness of what he suspected of its absence.

The word "a people" (qawman) was added and he did not limit himself to "you are ignorant," to indicate that ignorance had become firmly rooted in them, until it became one of the constituents of their peoplehood, and to indicate that it had encompassed the entire tribe, as Lot said to his people, ﴿Is there not among you a single rightly-guided man?﴾

The majority read "wa-ublighukum" with a doubled lam. Abu 'Amr read it with a single lam. It is said: "ballagha al-khabar" with the doubling and "ablaghahu" with the hamza, when one makes it reach (its destination).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 46, verse 24–25:

[49]
﴿When they saw it as a cloud coming towards their valleys, they said: "This is a cloud bringing us rain." Nay, it is that which you were seeking to hasten: a wind in which is a painful punishment,﴾ ﴿destroying everything by the command of its Lord, so that by morning nothing could be seen but their dwellings. Thus do We recompense the criminal people.﴾

The fa' (فاء) here marks the continuation of the rest of the story from what has been mentioned of it, meaning: when God willed to visit them with the punishment and they saw it as a cloud, they said, "This is a cloud..." to the end. There is therefore an implied elision in the speech that the context indicates, and this type of continuation is called fa'a sihah (فَصِيحَة, the "eloquent" fa'). The narrative of what occurred between their denial of Hud and the descent of the punishment upon them has been omitted. It is mentioned in the books of Arab history that a severe drought afflicted them for years, and that Hud separated from them, went out to Mecca and died there. It has also been said that he was buried in al-Hijr around the Ka'bah, as was mentioned in the commentary on Surat al-Hijr.

Their saying, "This is a cloud bringing us rain," indicates that they were in need of rain. In Surat Hud there is Hud's saying to them: ﴿And, O my people, ask forgiveness of your Lord and then turn back to Him; He will send down the sky upon you in abundant rain﴾ [Hud: 52], and their story is set out in full in our commentary on Surat Hud.

The pronoun in "ra'awhu" (رَأوْهُ) refers to "ma ta'iduna" (what you threaten us with), namely the punishment. The pronoun for the punishment is applied to what was seen, because what was seen is the cause of the punishment, which is what the wind carried. "'Aridan" (عارِضًا) is a circumstantial accusative (ḥāl) from it, and "al-'arid" (العارِض) is the cloud that spreads across the sky's expanse, i.e. they saw it as something spread across the horizon. The intended meaning is not a cloud of rain, because it was not so, and how could it be, since his saying "Nay, it is that which you were seeking to hasten: a wind" nullifies their saying "This is a cloud bringing us rain."

"Mustaqbila awdiyatihim" (مُسْتَقْبِلَ أوْدِيَتِهِمْ) is an adjective (na't) of "'aridin" (عارِضٍ).

Al-istiqbal (الِاسْتِقْبال) is facing towards something opposite it, i.e. moving towards their valleys.

"Awdiyah" (أوْدِيَةٌ) is the plural of "wad" (وادٍ) in a rare plural pattern like "nad" and "andiyah". The word "wadi" (valley) is used, in a predominant usage, for the abode and dwelling-place of a people, because most of their dwellings were on plains and near water. In the hadith of Sa'd ibn Mu'adh in Mecca after the Hijrah, and what passed between him and Abu Jahl of exchange and raising of voice against Abu Jahl, Umayyah said to him: "Do not raise your voice against Abu al-Hakam, the lord of the people of the valley (sayyid ahl al-wadi)." He pluralised "awdiyah" in view of the multitude and spread of their dwellings.

[50]
"Al-'arid" in their saying "This is a cloud bringing us rain" is the great cloud that appears on the horizon like a mountain, and "mumtirunа" (مُمْطِرُنا) is an adjective of "'arid".

His saying "Nay, it is that which you were seeking to hasten" (بَلْ هو ما اسْتَعْجَلْتُمْ بِهِ) is a quotation (maqul) of an elided saying. It may be from the words of Hud, if Hud was among them and had not left for Mecca before that; or it may be from the words of one of their men who saw the signs of evil in that cloud. It has been said: the speaker was Bakr ibn Mu'awiyah of the people of 'Ad, who said when he saw it: "Indeed I see a cloud blackened, it will leave none of 'Ad alive." Perhaps the truth became clear to him from Hud's warning when he saw a cloud unlike what was familiar; but it did not benefit him after the punishment had descended upon them. Or he had believed earlier, and God saved him from the punishment by an extraordinary means.

The verb of saying was elided in order to present the speaker of the words as though present at the time of the descent of this verse, having heard their speech and known their delusion, so he spoke these words to startle them. This is from the evocation of a wondrous situation, like the saying of Malik ibn al-Rayb:

"Desire called me, from my folk, my kin and neighbours, at Dhi al-Shayyatayn; so I turned back behind me."

He imagined a caller calling him, so he turned; and this is from imagination (takhayyul) in eloquent speech.

The punishment is made to be enclosed within the wind as an intensification of causation, because the relation of container and contained is more intimate than the relation of cause and effect. "Tadmir" (التَّدْمِيرُ) is destruction, as has been previously discussed.

"Kull shay'" (كُلُّ شَيْءٍ) is used for the multitude of things, for "kull" often occurs in their speech in the sense of multitude. It was discussed earlier at His saying, Exalted is He, "Even if every sign came to them" in Surat Yunus.

The meaning: it destroys whatever is of the kind that the wind destroys, of humans, animals and dwellings.

His saying "bi-amri rabbiha" (بِأمْرِ رَبِّها) is a circumstantial phrase (hal) from the pronoun in "tudammiru". The benefit of this circumstance is to bring close the manner of its destruction of everything, i.e. a wondrous destruction by means of the command of its Lord, meaning His subjecting things to it; so the bā' is causal.

[51]
The Lord is attributed to the pronoun of the wind because it is subjected to the command of divine creation; so "the command" here is the command of creation (amr al-takwin).

"Fa-asbahu" (فَأصْبَحُوا) means "they became", and "asbaha" here is among the sisters of "sara". It is not meant that their destruction occurred at night, for they were destroyed over days and nights; some of them perished in the morning and some perished in the evening and at night.

The address in His saying "la tara" (لا تَرى) is to whoever could see at that time, completing the evocation of the wondrous state of their ruin, as though the verse were being revealed at the time of this event.

By "masakin" (المَساكِن) is meant their traces, remains and debris after the wind had uprooted most of them.

The meaning: the wind came upon all of them, and none of the inhabitants of their dwellings remained.

His saying "Thus do We recompense the criminal people" (كَذَلِكَ نَجْزِي القَوْمَ المُجْرِمِينَ) means: like the recompense of 'Ad, We recompense the criminal people. It is a threat to the polytheists of Quraysh, a warning to them, and a preparation for His saying "And We had established them in that wherein We have not established you."

The majority read "la tara" with the feminine second-person prefix (تَرى), in the active voice, with "masakinahum" in the accusative. 'Asim, Hamzah and Khalaf read it with a yā' (يَاء) prefix in the passive voice, with "masakinuhum" in the nominative. They applied to the plural the form of the third-person masculine singular, because the plural is excepted by "illa" (إلّا), which separates it from the verb.

This is a deduction drawn from the admonition of the polytheists through the example of ʿĀd, so that they may know that the One who was able to destroy ʿĀd is able to destroy those who are less than them in strength and number, and so that they may know that these people were like them, possessing the faculties of intellect and sense, and that they neglected to benefit from their faculties, so they denied the signs of God, [p. 52] and mocked them and His threat, so there befell them what they used to mock. The Quraysh know that their state is like the state recounted concerning those people, so let them prepare for what will befall them.

To serve this deduction, the style of speech was changed to address the polytheists of Mecca. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) from the wāw of the group in the words ﴿قالوا أجئتنا﴾ [they said: "Have you come to us?"], and the statement is used to express wonder at their failure to benefit from the gifts of their intellects.

The emphasis of this statement with the oath particle (lām al-qasam), although its meaning is beyond doubt, is directed toward intensifying the expression of wonder.

Al-tamkīn (establishing/granting power): giving makna, with a fatḥa on the mīm and a kasra on the kāf, which means power and strength. It is said: makkana min kadhā and tamakkana minhu, when one is able to do something. It is also said: makkanahu fī kadhā, when one grants him the capacity over what follows the particle of location (ḥarf al-ẓarfiyya), and it is interpreted according to what suits that location. God, the Exalted, said: ﴿makkannāhum fī al-arḍ mā lam numakkin lakum﴾ [We had established them on the earth in what We have not established you in], in Sūrat al-Anʿām.

So the meaning is: We gave them capacity in that in which We did not give you capacity, that is, in all that peoples and nations are given capacity in. This was discussed earlier at His saying, ﴿Have they not seen how many generations We destroyed before them, whom We had established on the earth﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:6], at the beginning of al-Anʿām, so what is here is joined to it.

The مَا in قوله "فيما" is a relative pronoun (mawṣūla). The إن is a negative particle, meaning: in that which We did not establish you in.

The meaning of "We established you in it" is: We established you in its like or its kind, for the genera and species of beings are immaterial realities whose gifts do not change, and they differ only by their existence in particulars. Therefore it was appropriate for the verb makkannākum to be followed by the particle of location, with a pronoun referring to the relative pronoun that covers the things in which ʿĀd were given power.

Among the eloquent features of the composition is that the negation came here with the particle إن (in), although negation with it is less frequently used than negation with ما (mā), intentionally here to avoid the repugnance of two similar sounds in succession, namely ما الموصولة and ما النافية, even though their meanings differ. Do you not see that the Arabs substituted the hāʾ for the alif in مهما? Its original form was ما ما, composed of the particle of location ما and the superfluous ما which adds the conditional sense, like أينما. Al-Zamakhsharī said in al-Kashshāf: Abū al-Ṭayyib [al-Mutanabbī] indeed erred in his saying:

*"By your life, what (mā) departed from you for a striker"*

I say: Ibn Jinnī and others who explained the Dīwān before al-Mutanabbī did not take issue with him. A similar usage occurred in the poetic necessities (ḍarūrāt) of the earlier poets, such as the saying of Khiṭām al-Mujāshiʿī:

*"And scorched ones, like what (kamā) is set upon three stones"*

It is not excusable for later (muwallad) poets.

As for when ما is a negative particle and the speaker intends to emphasize it with verbal emphasis (taʾkīd lafẓī), then the bringing of the particle إن after ما is more fitting, as in the saying of al-Nābigha:

*"Ashes like the kohl of the eye, which I can scarcely make out, and a boundary of a pool, broken and humbled."*

The benefit of his saying "and We gave them hearing, sight, and hearts" is that nothing that could impair their perception of the truth was lacking from them, had it not been for obstinacy. This is an allusion to the polytheists of Quraysh, meaning: you have deprived yourselves of benefiting from your hearing, your sight, and your intellects, just as they were deprived, and the condition is identical and the cause is identical, so it is likely that the requital will be the same.

The singling out of hearing alone, apart from sight and hearts, is for the reason mentioned earlier at His saying, ﴿Say: Have you considered if God were to take away your hearing and your sight﴾ [al-Anʿām 6:46], in Sūrat al-Anʿām, and His saying, ﴿Who controls hearing and sight?﴾ [Yūnus 10:31], in Sūrat Yūnus.

The مِن in His saying "min shay'" is superfluous (zāʾida), for the explicit negation of the genus, so for this reason the word shay', governed by the superfluous min, takes the place of the absolute object (mafʿūl muṭlaq), because what is meant by shay' is a kind of giving benefit, and the proper case of shay' is the accusative, but it was put in the genitive by the entry of the superfluous particle of governance.

[p. 54] The إذ is an adverb of time, meaning: the period of their denial, and it is used here in the sense of causation, since the meaning of the time adverb and the meaning of causation are equivalent, for when He made the thing of benefit dependent on the time of their denial of God's signs, as is understood from the annexation of إذ to the clause after it, it was known that that time has an effect on the negation of benefit.

God's signs are the indications of His will, from the miracles of their Messenger, and from the proofs that point to the truth of what he called them to.

Their example applies to the state of the polytheists, for they denied the signs of God, which are the signs of the Qur'an, since it combined the true reality of the signs in both senses.

Wa-ḥāqa bihim: encompassed them. "What they used to mock" is the punishment. He turned away from its explicit name to the relative pronoun in order to draw attention to their error and the badness of their outlook.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 46, verse 27:

﴿And We had already destroyed the towns around you, and We varied the signs, so that they might return.﴾

He follows the mention of the parable of 'Ad with their messenger by stating that this parable is not unique in its kind. God destroyed other peoples from among their neighbours whose conditions resembled the conditions of the polytheists. He reminded them that their towns were near them, known to those who know them and heard of by those who have not seen them. These are the towns of Thamud, the people of Lot, the companions of the Thicket (al-Aykah), Saba', and the people of Tubba'. The clause is coordinated with the clause "and mention the brother of 'Ad" and so on. The destruction of the peoples is expressed by the destruction of their towns (kinaya, a figurative allusion, in which the intended meaning is stated indirectly), as an intensification (mubalagha, hyperbole) of their total annihilation, because when a town is destroyed no one of its people remains. Similarly, 'Antara expressed the shaking of the body by the shaking of the garments (kinaya) in his saying:

"So I pierced with the solid spear his garments."

From this is God's saying, exalted is He: ﴿And your garments, purify﴾ (al-Muddaththir 74:4).

The "variation of the signs" (tasrif al-ayat) means diversifying them according to the aim intended by them, which is abandoning polytheism and denying the messengers. The original meaning of tasrif is change and alteration, since it derives from sarf, which means turning away. It is used here (as a kinaya) for clarification and explanation, because the multiplicity of kinds of evidence increases the intended meaning in clarity.

The meaning of the variation of the signs is that they are sometimes by way of argument and rational debate, sometimes by way of threat against the deed, another time by way of warning, and at other times by way of reminding of blessings and giving thanks for them. The clause ﴿so that they might return﴾ is a resumptive sentence (isti'naf, a new independent sentence) expressing hope (tarajji), and its position is that of an object of purpose, meaning: in hope of their return.

Here "return" is used figuratively (majaz, metaphorical usage) for abandoning what they are engaged in of polytheism and obstinacy. Hope from God, exalted is He, is used figuratively for demand, meaning: as an extension to them and a respite, so that they may reflect and take heed. This is an allusion (ta'rid, indirect reference) to the polytheists of Makkah, for they are alike in the varieties of the variation of the signs, in addition to what was varied for them of the signs of the inimitability of the Qur'an. The discussion of (la'alla) in the speech of God has preceded at the beginning of al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 46, verse 28:

﴿Why then did those whom they had taken as gods besides Allah, for nearness (to Allah), not help them? Rather, they vanished from them. That was their falsehood and what they used to fabricate.﴾

This follows from what preceded of admonition through the punishment of 'Ad, described in detail, and the punishment of the people of the towns, described in brief. There follows a rebuke directed at their gods, for they sat aloof from helping them and rescuing them from the power of Allah. The intended purpose is to direct the rebuke at the destroyed nations, by way of the method of directing a prohibition, or something similar, at one other than the one prohibited, so that the one prohibited avoids the causes of what is forbidden, as in their saying: "I should not find you doing such-and-such," and "I should not see you here."

The intended purpose of this rebuke is to correct the nations who took idols for victory and repelling (harm). This is used allusively toward the listeners who resemble them in worshipping gods besides Allah, completing the admonition and rebuke by way of comparison and analogical likening. For this reason he follows it with his saying "Rather, they vanished from them," because the rebuke amounts to the sense of negating help.

When the particle (lawla) enters upon a verbal clause, its original meaning is exhortation (tahdid), that is, urging the doer of the verb that follows (lawla) to bring about that act. When the doer is not the one addressed in the speech, (lawla) signifies rebuke or something similar, since there is no benefit in urging the addressee to perform the act of another.

The use of the relative pronoun (alladhina) serves, because of what the relative clause contains, to draw attention to the error and mistake in their worship of idols, which therefore did not avail them anything, as in the saying of 'Abda ibn al-Tabib:

Those whom you see as your brothers,
The relief of their hearts is that you be struck down.

The idols were treated as rational beings by applying to them the plural of rational beings, following the prevailing usage of the Arabs, as has been mentioned more than once before.

"Qurbanan" is a verbal noun on the pattern of "ghufran," in the accusative as an object of purpose, reporting their known claim recounted in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who take protectors besides Him say: "We only worship them that they may bring us nearer to Allah in closeness."﴾ [al-Zumar: 3]. This verbal noun is parenthetical between "ittakhadhu" and its object, and "min dun Allah" is connected to "ittakhadhu." "Dun" here means distance, that is, transgressing Allah by taking the idols as gods, and this is a report of their condition in order to increase its ugliness and reproach.

"Bal" here has the sense of "lakin" (but), a turning away and an exceptive correction following the rebuke, since it carries the sense of negation. That is: those whom they took as gods did not help them, nor did they bring them near to Allah so as to repel the punishment from them; rather, they vanished from them, that is, they were absent from them at the time the punishment descended upon them.

The root meaning of "dalal" is failure to find the way, and it is figuratively used for lack of benefit despite presence, as an ironic metaphor: that is, they were absent from them, though had they been present they would have helped them. This is similar to the irony in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it will be said: "Call your partners," and they will call them, but they will not respond to them﴾ [al-Qasas: 64], in Surat al-Qasas.

As for His saying "That was their falsehood," it is a summing-up of the whole clause "Why then did those whom they had taken as gods besides Allah...," and it is an indication of the ironic metaphor in His saying "they vanished from them."

The demonstrative "dhalika" refers to what is contained in His saying "those whom they had taken as gods besides Allah, for nearness," namely, one who claims that idols are gods and that they bring them near to Allah. "Ifk" (with a kasra on the hamza) and "iftira'" are a kind of lying, namely inventing false reports, and it is synonymous with "ikhtilaq," because it is derived from "fary al-jild" (cutting the hide). So "iftira'" is the lie that one utters. Therefore the conjunction of "ma kanu yaftarun" to "ifkihim" is conjunction of the more specific to the more general, for their claim that idols are partners of Allah is a lie already related earlier, and thus it is an ifk. As for their claim that they bring them near to Allah, that is an iftira' which they invented.

The insertion of the verb "kanu" indicates that their fabrication is deeply rooted in them. The use of "yaftarun" in the present form indicates that their fabrication is repeated.

This is a confirmation for the Prophet ﷺ, that God made the jinn subservient to believe in him and in the Qur'an. Thus the Messenger of God ﷺ was confirmed among both the two weighty groups (humans and jinn) and honoured among the worlds, and this is something that had not been granted to any messenger before him.

The purpose of the Qur'an's report about the jinn is to rebuke the polytheists: the jinn, who are from another world, knew the Qur'an and were certain that it is from God, while the polytheists, who are from the world of humans, of the same kind as the Messenger ﷺ who was sent with the Qur'an, and who speak the language of the Qur'an, have continued in doubt, denial and obstinacy. This is therefore an admonition to the polytheists by way of contrast with their own condition, after their admonition had already come through the case of their counterparts in disbelief from among their own kind.

The occasion for mentioning the belief of the jinn is what preceded in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are the ones against whom the word has come true, among nations that passed away before them of jinn and humans; indeed they were losers.﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 18]

So this sentence is coordinated with the sentence "and mention the brother of 'Ad" (Al-Ahqaf: 21), a coordination of narrative with narrative. The phrase "when We turned" here is connected to a verb implied by his words "and mention the brother of 'Ad" [Al-Ahqaf: 21]. The estimated sense is: "And mention when We turned towards you a company of jinn."

God commanded His Messenger ﷺ to recount this to the polytheists, even though they would not believe him, in order to record that this news reached them, so that whoever is guided may benefit from it, and so that the consequence may be written against those who are not guided.

The exegetes differed concerning this verse as to whether the jinn were present with the knowledge of the Prophet ﷺ or without his knowledge. In the Jami' of al-Tirmidhi, it is related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ did not recite to the jinn, nor did he see them. The Messenger of God set out with a group of his companions, intending Souk 'Ukaz. When they were at Nakhla (a place-name), while he was leading his companions in the dawn prayer, a company of jinn was there. When they heard the Qur'an, they returned to their people and said: 'We have heard a wondrous Qur'an.'"

In the Sahih, it is related from Ibn Mas'ud: "We missed the Prophet ﷺ one night while he was in Mecca, so we said: 'What has happened to him? Has he been abducted or taken by the ghouls?' We spent the worst night until, when we woke in the morning, behold, he came to us from the direction of Hira. He said: 'The caller of the jinn came to me, so I went to them and recited the Qur'an to them.'"

Whatever the case, this event is an extraordinary occurrence and is a miracle of the Prophet ﷺ. God's words, may He be exalted, ﴿O assembly of jinn and humans, did there not come to you messengers from among you, relating to you My signs﴾ [Al-An'am: 130], have already preceded in Surat al-An'am.

"Al-Sarf" means dispatch.

"Al-Nafar" means a number of people fewer than twenty. Its application to the jinn is because they are treated in the position of humans, and it is clarified by his words "from the jinn."

The clause "listening to the Qur'an" is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) concerning "the jinn." Since the circumstantial clause is a restriction on its governing verb, which is "We turned," the estimated sense becomes: "they listen from you when they are present." Thus this functions as a purpose clause (maf'ul li-ajlihi). The meaning is: "We turned them towards you so that they might listen to the Qur'an."

The pronoun in "when they were present" (hadaru-hu) refers to the Qur'an. The transitive use of the verb "were present" with the Qur'an's pronoun is a figurative (majaz) transitivity, because they were in fact present with the reciter of the Qur'an, who is the Messenger ﷺ.

"Be silent" (ansitu) is a command to direct the ears towards speech with attention, so that nothing of it is missed.

[Page 59 begins here]

In the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, during the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "Ask the people to be silent," that is, before he began his sermon.

In the hadith: "If you say to your companion on Friday, 'Be silent,' while the imam is delivering the sermon, you have engaged in idle talk." That is, they all said: "Be silent," each one saying it to the rest, out of eagerness for attentiveness, so they all uttered it together.

"Qudiya" is in the passive voice with an implied agent. The pronoun refers to the Qur'an by an estimated genitive: "its recitation was concluded," that is, the Prophet ﷺ finished the recitation when they were present. With his finishing the recitation, God's purpose in turning the jinn to listen to the Qur'an was accomplished, "so they turned," that is, they departed from the place of listening and returned to where their kind is, which is what is expressed by "their people," in the manner of metaphor (majaz). It was treated in the position of humankind because of this state, which resembles the state of people. So applying "people" (qawm) to the nation of jinn is like applying "company" (nafar) to the group of jinn who were turned towards listening to the Qur'an.

"Al-mundhir" means one who gives news of a frightening matter.

The meaning of "they returned to their people as warners" is that they returned to the members of their kind after having been in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ listening to the Qur'an, and they informed them of what they had heard of the Qur'an, of what contains warning of the wrath of God, the Exalted, for whoever does not believe in the Qur'an.

Giving good tidings is for whoever acts upon what the Qur'an brought.

There is no doubt that God facilitated for them their presence for the recitation of a chapter comprehensive of what the Qur'an brought, like the Opening of the Book and Surat al-Ikhlas.

The clause "They said, 'O our people...'" to its end explains His words "warners."

The narration of the jinn's address with these words, which is in Arabic speech, is a narration in meaning, since it is not known that the jinn have knowledge of human speech. Likewise the verb "they said" is a metaphor for conveying, that is, they conveyed to their kind, by the means of understanding that they have, the meanings of what is related in this verse by speech, just as in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿An ant said: "O ants, enter your dwellings."﴾

They began conveying to them that they had heard a Book, as a preliminary to the purpose of admonition, by mentioning the Book and describing it, so that the addressees would be eager for what follows.

[Page 60 begins here]

They described the Book as having been revealed "after Moses" rather than "revealed to Muhammad ﷺ," because the Torah is the last book of the books of legislation that descended before the Qur'an. As for what came after it, these are books that complete the Torah and clarify it, such as the Psalms of David and the Gospel of Jesus. So it was as though nothing new had descended after the Torah. When the Qur'an descended, it came with an independent guidance, not intended primarily to clarify the Torah, but it confirms the Torah and guides to more than what the Torah guided to.

"What lies between its hands" means what preceded it of the true religions.

The meaning of "guiding to the truth" is guiding to correct belief, opposed to falsehood, including monotheism and what is obligatory for God, may He be exalted, of attributes and what is impossible to ascribe to Him.

The intended sense of "the straight path" is what is followed in deeds and dealings, and what results from that of reward. It is likened to the straight path, whose traveller does not stray from the aim of his journey.

It is also possible that "the truth" is meant to include belief and righteous deeds, and that "the straight path" is meant to refer to the proofs indicating the truth and exposing falsehood, for they are like the straight path in conveying their followers to knowledge of the truth.

Their repeating the call to "O our people" is for the sake of emphasis on what follows the call, which is "respond to the caller of God," to its end, because that is the intended purpose of directing the address to their people. The intended purpose is not to inform their people of the wondrous events they encountered; rather, that was a preliminary to this. Also, because the difference of aims and the renewal of purpose require repeating such a call, just as the orator repeats "O people," as occurred in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage.

"Respond" (ajibu) is used figuratively (isti'arah, metaphor) for the meaning of "act" and "undertake," likening action to the response to a caller in the speech of a speaker, as in the verse: ﴿Except that I called you and you responded to me,﴾ that is, except that I commanded you and you obeyed me. For their people were not summoned by anyone to anything; the meaning is: obey what is asked of you to do.

"The caller of God" may refer to the Qur'an, since it was mentioned before in their words: "we have heard a Book revealed after Moses." The Qur'an was called "the caller of God" figuratively, because it includes a request to seek guidance by the guidance of God; this is likened to a call to God and a term describing the Qur'an is derived from it, namely "caller of God," by way of subordinate metaphor (tabaiyyah), which follows the metaphor of "respond" in the sense of "act."

[Page 61 begins here]

"The caller of God" may also refer to Muhammad ﷺ, since he calls to God by means of the Qur'an.

The conjunction of "and believe in Him" with "respond to the caller of God" is a conjunction of the particular with the general.

The pronoun in "in Him" refers to God, that is, "and believe in God," which is the more appropriate reading given the coherence of pronouns with "He will forgive you your sins and protect you from a painful punishment." Or it refers to "the caller of God," that is, "believe in what is in it," or "believe in what he brought." On the last two possibilities, this implies that these jinn are commanded to submit to Islam.

The "min" in "from your sins" is most evidently causal (ta'lil), so it relates to "respond," considering that the response is answered by "He will forgive." It may also be partitive (tab'idiyyah), that is, "He will forgive you some of your sins." In that case, this is a hedge in the promise, because they had not fully ascertained the details of which sins are forgiven and which are not, since they had heard only part of the Qur'an and had not comprehended all that is in it.

It may also be superfluous, for emphasis, according to a group who hold that "min" may be added in affirmative sentences just as it is added in negative ones.

As for the "min" in "and protect you from a painful punishment," it is for the transitivity of the verb "protect you," since it is said: "he protected him from the injustice of so-and-so," meaning he prevented him and kept him away.

God's reporting of this from the jinn is an affirmation of what they said. It indicates that the jinn have comprehension of meanings, and that what the rational proofs indicate concerning theological matters is obligatory for the jinn to believe, because the basis of legal responsibility for rational theology is comprehension. It also indicates that the known matters must be believed when they reach their faculties or when they are alerted to them, as the story of Iblis indicates. These jinn were alerted to them by being turned to listen to the Qur'an, and they alerted their people to them by conveying what they had heard of the Qur'an. According to this meaning, reward and punishment follow: as He said, may He be exalted: ﴿I shall surely fill Hell with jinn and humans altogether﴾ [Hud: 119], and He said in address to Satan: ﴿I shall surely fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you of them, all together﴾ [Sad: 85]. As for the branches of the Sharia, they are not suitable for the species of jinn. The apparent meaning of the verse is that those to whom the call of the Qur'an has reached are held accountable if they do not act upon it, and that they will be punished.

[Page 62 begins here]

The scholars differed concerning the jinn's reward for good deeds. Abu Hanifa said: the jinn have no reward except that they are protected from the punishment of the Fire, and then they are told: "Become dust, like the beasts." Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ibn Abi Layla and al-Dahhak said: just as they are recompensed for evil, they are recompensed for good, and so they enter Paradise. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) reported that a debate took place on this question between Abu Hanifa and Malik, and I have not seen it from anyone else.

This is a question with no benefit, and a Muslim is not obliged to hold any belief concerning it, except that a scholar, when the verses pass by him, is required to understand them.

The meaning of "then he cannot escape in the earth" is that he will not escape the punishment of God for not responding to His caller. So the object of "escape" (mu'jiz) is implied, indicated by the genitive in "the caller of God": the estimated sense is "he is not one who escapes God." In Surat al-Jinn He said: ﴿that we shall never escape God in the earth nor escape Him by fleeing﴾ [Al-Jinn: 12], which is a negation that one who seeks Him could make Him incapable, that is, could escape the power of God over him. The statement is a metonymy (kinayah) for being held accountable with punishment.

The intended sense of "in the earth" is the generalization of directions. It follows the style of Arabic usage; otherwise the place of the jinn is not specified.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on the verse: "And he will have no protectors besides Him" (﴿ولَيْسَ لَهُ مِن دُونِهِ أولِياءُ﴾), that is, no helper who would support him against Allah and shield him from Him. This is a negation that he has any way to salvation by seeking refuge in a place beyond the reach of Allah's power, or by seeking protection from someone able to shield him from the punishment of Allah. The mention of this is an allusion (ta'rid) to the polytheists.

The demonstrative in "Those are in manifest error" (﴿أُولَئِكَ في ضَلالٍ مُبِينٍ﴾) serves to draw attention to the fact that those whose condition is this deserve the judgment that follows the demonstrative, because of what precedes the demonstrative as its cause, as in His saying "Those are upon guidance from their Lord" (﴿أُولَئِكَ عَلى هُدًى مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾) [al-Baqarah: 5].

The sense of location (zarfiyyah) derived from "in error" (﴿فِي ضَلالٍ مُبِينٍ﴾) is figurative, to convey the intensity of their being immersed in error, as though they were in a vessel that is error itself.

Al-mubin (the manifest) means the clear, because it is an error against which the proofs and evidences have established that it is false.
