In the hadith of Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, during the Farewell Pilgrimage, the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "Ask the people to be silent," that is, before he began his sermon.

In the hadith: "If you say to your companion on Friday, 'Be silent,' while the imam is delivering the sermon, you have engaged in idle talk." That is, they all said: "Be silent," each one saying it to the rest, out of eagerness for attentiveness, so they all uttered it together.

"Qudiya" is in the passive voice with an implied agent. The pronoun refers to the Qur'an by an estimated genitive: "its recitation was concluded," that is, the Prophet ﷺ finished the recitation when they were present. With his finishing the recitation, God's purpose in turning the jinn to listen to the Qur'an was accomplished, "so they turned," that is, they departed from the place of listening and returned to where their kind is, which is what is expressed by "their people," in the manner of metaphor (majaz). It was treated in the position of humankind because of this state, which resembles the state of people. So applying "people" (qawm) to the nation of jinn is like applying "company" (nafar) to the group of jinn who were turned towards listening to the Qur'an.

"Al-mundhir" means one who gives news of a frightening matter.

The meaning of "they returned to their people as warners" is that they returned to the members of their kind after having been in the presence of the Prophet ﷺ listening to the Qur'an, and they informed them of what they had heard of the Qur'an, of what contains warning of the wrath of God, the Exalted, for whoever does not believe in the Qur'an.

Giving good tidings is for whoever acts upon what the Qur'an brought.

There is no doubt that God facilitated for them their presence for the recitation of a chapter comprehensive of what the Qur'an brought, like the Opening of the Book and Surat al-Ikhlas.

The clause "They said, 'O our people...'" to its end explains His words "warners."

The narration of the jinn's address with these words, which is in Arabic speech, is a narration in meaning, since it is not known that the jinn have knowledge of human speech. Likewise the verb "they said" is a metaphor for conveying, that is, they conveyed to their kind, by the means of understanding that they have, the meanings of what is related in this verse by speech, just as in His words, may He be exalted: ﴿An ant said: "O ants, enter your dwellings."﴾

They began conveying to them that they had heard a Book, as a preliminary to the purpose of admonition, by mentioning the Book and describing it, so that the addressees would be eager for what follows.

[Page 60 begins here]

They described the Book as having been revealed "after Moses" rather than "revealed to Muhammad ﷺ," because the Torah is the last book of the books of legislation that descended before the Qur'an. As for what came after it, these are books that complete the Torah and clarify it, such as the Psalms of David and the Gospel of Jesus. So it was as though nothing new had descended after the Torah. When the Qur'an descended, it came with an independent guidance, not intended primarily to clarify the Torah, but it confirms the Torah and guides to more than what the Torah guided to.

"What lies between its hands" means what preceded it of the true religions.

The meaning of "guiding to the truth" is guiding to correct belief, opposed to falsehood, including monotheism and what is obligatory for God, may He be exalted, of attributes and what is impossible to ascribe to Him.

The intended sense of "the straight path" is what is followed in deeds and dealings, and what results from that of reward. It is likened to the straight path, whose traveller does not stray from the aim of his journey.

It is also possible that "the truth" is meant to include belief and righteous deeds, and that "the straight path" is meant to refer to the proofs indicating the truth and exposing falsehood, for they are like the straight path in conveying their followers to knowledge of the truth.

Their repeating the call to "O our people" is for the sake of emphasis on what follows the call, which is "respond to the caller of God," to its end, because that is the intended purpose of directing the address to their people. The intended purpose is not to inform their people of the wondrous events they encountered; rather, that was a preliminary to this. Also, because the difference of aims and the renewal of purpose require repeating such a call, just as the orator repeats "O people," as occurred in the sermon of the Farewell Pilgrimage.

"Respond" (ajibu) is used figuratively (isti'arah, metaphor) for the meaning of "act" and "undertake," likening action to the response to a caller in the speech of a speaker, as in the verse: ﴿Except that I called you and you responded to me,﴾ that is, except that I commanded you and you obeyed me. For their people were not summoned by anyone to anything; the meaning is: obey what is asked of you to do.

"The caller of God" may refer to the Qur'an, since it was mentioned before in their words: "we have heard a Book revealed after Moses." The Qur'an was called "the caller of God" figuratively, because it includes a request to seek guidance by the guidance of God; this is likened to a call to God and a term describing the Qur'an is derived from it, namely "caller of God," by way of subordinate metaphor (tabaiyyah), which follows the metaphor of "respond" in the sense of "act."

[Page 61 begins here]

"The caller of God" may also refer to Muhammad ﷺ, since he calls to God by means of the Qur'an.

The conjunction of "and believe in Him" with "respond to the caller of God" is a conjunction of the particular with the general.

The pronoun in "in Him" refers to God, that is, "and believe in God," which is the more appropriate reading given the coherence of pronouns with "He will forgive you your sins and protect you from a painful punishment." Or it refers to "the caller of God," that is, "believe in what is in it," or "believe in what he brought." On the last two possibilities, this implies that these jinn are commanded to submit to Islam.

The "min" in "from your sins" is most evidently causal (ta'lil), so it relates to "respond," considering that the response is answered by "He will forgive." It may also be partitive (tab'idiyyah), that is, "He will forgive you some of your sins." In that case, this is a hedge in the promise, because they had not fully ascertained the details of which sins are forgiven and which are not, since they had heard only part of the Qur'an and had not comprehended all that is in it.

It may also be superfluous, for emphasis, according to a group who hold that "min" may be added in affirmative sentences just as it is added in negative ones.

As for the "min" in "and protect you from a painful punishment," it is for the transitivity of the verb "protect you," since it is said: "he protected him from the injustice of so-and-so," meaning he prevented him and kept him away.

God's reporting of this from the jinn is an affirmation of what they said. It indicates that the jinn have comprehension of meanings, and that what the rational proofs indicate concerning theological matters is obligatory for the jinn to believe, because the basis of legal responsibility for rational theology is comprehension. It also indicates that the known matters must be believed when they reach their faculties or when they are alerted to them, as the story of Iblis indicates. These jinn were alerted to them by being turned to listen to the Qur'an, and they alerted their people to them by conveying what they had heard of the Qur'an. According to this meaning, reward and punishment follow: as He said, may He be exalted: ﴿I shall surely fill Hell with jinn and humans altogether﴾ [Hud: 119], and He said in address to Satan: ﴿I shall surely fill Hell with you and with whoever follows you of them, all together﴾ [Sad: 85]. As for the branches of the Sharia, they are not suitable for the species of jinn. The apparent meaning of the verse is that those to whom the call of the Qur'an has reached are held accountable if they do not act upon it, and that they will be punished.

[Page 62 begins here]

The scholars differed concerning the jinn's reward for good deeds. Abu Hanifa said: the jinn have no reward except that they are protected from the punishment of the Fire, and then they are told: "Become dust, like the beasts." Malik, al-Shafi'i, Ibn Abi Layla and al-Dahhak said: just as they are recompensed for evil, they are recompensed for good, and so they enter Paradise. Al-Fakhr (al-Razi) reported that a debate took place on this question between Abu Hanifa and Malik, and I have not seen it from anyone else.

This is a question with no benefit, and a Muslim is not obliged to hold any belief concerning it, except that a scholar, when the verses pass by him, is required to understand them.

The meaning of "then he cannot escape in the earth" is that he will not escape the punishment of God for not responding to His caller. So the object of "escape" (mu'jiz) is implied, indicated by the genitive in "the caller of God": the estimated sense is "he is not one who escapes God." In Surat al-Jinn He said: ﴿that we shall never escape God in the earth nor escape Him by fleeing﴾ [Al-Jinn: 12], which is a negation that one who seeks Him could make Him incapable, that is, could escape the power of God over him. The statement is a metonymy (kinayah) for being held accountable with punishment.

The intended sense of "in the earth" is the generalization of directions. It follows the style of Arabic usage; otherwise the place of the jinn is not specified.

Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on the verse: "And he will have no protectors besides Him" (﴿ولَيْسَ لَهُ مِن دُونِهِ أولِياءُ﴾), that is, no helper who would support him against Allah and shield him from Him. This is a negation that he has any way to salvation by seeking refuge in a place beyond the reach of Allah's power, or by seeking protection from someone able to shield him from the punishment of Allah. The mention of this is an allusion (ta'rid) to the polytheists.

The demonstrative in "Those are in manifest error" (﴿أُولَئِكَ في ضَلالٍ مُبِينٍ﴾) serves to draw attention to the fact that those whose condition is this deserve the judgment that follows the demonstrative, because of what precedes the demonstrative as its cause, as in His saying "Those are upon guidance from their Lord" (﴿أُولَئِكَ عَلى هُدًى مِن رَبِّهِمْ﴾) [al-Baqarah: 5].

The sense of location (zarfiyyah) derived from "in error" (﴿فِي ضَلالٍ مُبِينٍ﴾) is figurative, to convey the intensity of their being immersed in error, as though they were in a vessel that is error itself.

Al-mubin (the manifest) means the clear, because it is an error against which the proofs and evidences have established that it is false.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 46, verse 33:

﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth and was not wearied by their creation, is able to give life to the dead? Yes indeed! Verily, He is over all things Omnipotent.﴾ This is a return to the argument for the possibility of resurrection. It is connected to His words (﴿And he who says to his parents, "Fie upon you both! Do you promise me that I will be brought forth, when generations have passed before me?"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17]) up to His words ﴿Those are the ones against whom the Word has come into effect, among nations that passed away before them of jinn and men. Indeed, they were losers﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 18]. So it is a transition from admonition through the fate of their like among the nations to the argument refuting their error in associating partners with God, which is the error that emboldened them to deem resurrection impossible, after a lengthy refutation of the plurality of gods and of their denial of the Qur'an and their denial of the Prophet (ﷺ).

This is a return to the beginning, for the surah opened with the argument for resurrection in His words, exalted is He, ﴿We created not the heavens and the earth and what is between them except with truth﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 3], and the verse joins with His words "﴿And he who says to his parents, 'Fie upon you both! Do you promise me that I will be brought forth'﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17]" up to His words ﴿legends of the ancients﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 17].

The waw is conjunctive for the interrogative clause, and the interrogation is one of denunciation (inkari), and the seeing is cognitive ('ilmiyya). This verb was chosen from among the verbs of knowledge here because this knowledge has a clear, observable proof, namely the indication of the creation of the heavens and the earth from non-existence, and it is of the nature of this that the intellect is led to the conclusion that God is fully capable of what is less than that, namely giving life to the dead.

The particle (anna) with its noun and predicate occupies the position of the two objects of yarawu.

The superfluous ba' (al-ba' al-za'ida) entered upon the predicate of (anna), which is affirmative and emphatic, whereas the rule for the superfluous ba' is that it enters upon a negated predicate, because (anna) occurs within the predicate of a negation, namely "awa-lam yaraw."

(Bala) occurs as a response to the denunciatory interrogation. Do not be troubled by what is commonly stated on the tongues of the grammarians, that the denunciatory interrogation is in the sense of negation, and here it is connected to a verb negated by (lam), so that negating the negation becomes affirmation; thus the expected answer would be with the particle (na'am) rather than (bala), because the grammarians' statement meant only that it has the force of a negative for the one who asks with it, and they did not mean that it is treated as a negation in rulings. That something has the meaning of something else does not require that it be given all of its rulings.

The locus of wonder is the predicate of (anna). As for what precedes it, the polytheists do not deny it, so there is no wonder regarding it.

The ba' occurs in the predicate of (anna), "bi-qadir," on the basis that it is within the scope of negation, because the governing element, which is the particle (anna), occurs in the position of the two objects of the verb "yaraw," which is negated, so the negation spreads to the governing element and its operand, and therefore it is joined with the ba' for this reason. In the Kashshaf: "al-Zajjaj said: if you say, 'I did not think that Zayd is standing,' it is permissible; it is as if it were said, 'Is not God capable?'" End of quote.

Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash said: the ba' is superfluous for emphasis, like the ba' in His words ﴿And sufficient is God as a witness﴾ [al-Nisa': 79]; they mean that it is superfluous in affirmation in an exceptional manner.

As for the position of the response with the particle (bala), it is a response to an implied element indicated by the wonder at their supposition that God is not capable of giving life to the dead, for that contains a report about them that God does not give life to the dead; so He answered with His words "bala," teaching the Muslims and instructing them in what to answer them with.

Since the particle (bala) is a response, it stands in the place of a clause whose estimate is: He is capable of giving life to the dead.

The clause ﴿and was not wearied by their creation﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿who created the heavens and the earth﴾. His saying "lam yaya" is the present form of 'iya, of the pattern of radia, and its verbal noun is al-'iyy with a kasra on the ayn, which is inability to act or inability to speak, and from it comes al-'iyy in speech, meaning difficulty in expression.

Its transitivity with the ba' here is eloquent, to convey the negation of His inability in producing them and the negation of His inability in arranging their measures and their proportions; so the ba' of association was suitable for linking the creation to the inability in both its meanings.

Many lexicographers hold that al-'iyy is applied to fatigue, and to inability of opinion and inability of stratagem. According to al-Kisa'i and al-Asma'i: al-'iyy is specific to inability in stratagem and opinion. As for al-i'ya', it is fatigue from walking and the like, and its verb is a'ya, and this is what al-Raghib and the author of the Qamus followed.

The apparent sense of the Asas is that "a'ya" is only transitive, i.e., its hamza is the hamza of transitivity, so this is a third opinion.

Abu Hayyan claimed that its like is confined to what is heard. I say: this returns to the dispute over the two governing elements.

According to this opinion, His saying here, exalted is He, "wa-lam yaya," indicates the vastness of His knowledge, exalted is He, of the subtleties required by the order of the heavens and the earth in bringing them into existence fully fitted to it; and its indication of His power to create them is by way of implication (fahwa), or the matter of His power to create them is left to the knowledge of the addressees, since they did not deny that, and He intended only to alert them to the subtleties and wisdoms in the order of their creation, among which is the necessity of recompense for righteous deeds and evil deeds.

On this view also, the transitivity of the verb "ya'ya" with the ba' is determined.

Ya'qub read "bi-qadir" with a single ba' in the form of the active participle. Ya'qub read it as (yaqdir) with a ya' at its beginning, as a present verb from qudra, and the clause (yaqdir) would then be in the position of the predicate of (anna).

The clause ﴿Indeed, He is over all things Omnipotent﴾ is a concluding clause (tadhyil) for the clause "bala," because this one conveys the power to create the heavens and the earth, to give life to the dead, and other existents outside the heavens and the earth.

The emphasis of the statement with the particle (anna) is to refute their denial that God could give life to the dead, for when they deemed that impossible, they had denied the universality of His power over all things.

For this very point, the power to give life to the dead is expressed with the attribute qadir, and the power over all things is expressed with the attribute qadir, which is more indicative of power than the attribute qadir.

[p. 66]

The context of this statement is that the exposure of the polytheists to the Fire is one of the consequences of the recompense that follows the Resurrection. When the preceding verse mentioned the argument (*istidlal*) for the possibility of the Resurrection, it followed this with what will happen to them on the Day of Resurrection, combining argument and warning (*indhar*). It mentioned, from among this, what will be said to them, which they cannot avoid acknowledging as their error. This combines what they said in this world, "They said," with what they will admit within themselves on the Day of Recompense, by their saying, "Yes, by our Lord."

The sentence is conjoined (*'atf*) to the sentence ﴿Do they not see that God, who created the heavens and the earth...﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 33], and so on. The first part of the conjoined sentence is ﴿Is this not the truth?﴾ because it is the direct speech of an omitted verb of saying, whose implied meaning is: "And it will be said to those who disbelieved, on the day they are exposed to the Fire..."

Placing the time adverb before its governing verb is for the sake of emphasis on mentioning that day, to strengthen its fixing in minds.

Mentioning "those who disbelieved" as an explicit noun in place of a pronoun indicates, through the relative designation, the cause for the statement's construction: that it is said to them because they disbelieved.

The reference is to the torment of the Fire, as shown by His saying afterwards, ﴿He will say: Taste the torment.﴾

*Al-haqq* means the established, the firm.

The interrogation is rhetorical (*taqriri*), serving as a rebuke and reproach over what they used to claim, that the recompense is false and a lie, and that they said, ﴿and we will not be punished.﴾ They swore to their statement with an oath "by our Lord," an oath used to express regret and self-blame. They made the one sworn by the title of Lord out of tenderness and submission. He made their admission the basis for the command: ﴿Taste the torment.﴾ "Tasting" (*dhawq*) is a metaphor for perceiving. The imperative is used to express humiliation.

[p. 67]

﴿So be patient, as the resolute messengers from among the Messengers were patient, and do not seek to hasten [the punishment] for them. On the day they see what they are promised, it will seem to them that they had not remained [in the world] except for an hour of a day.﴾ This is a ramification (*tafrī'*, the drawing of a consequence from what precedes) of what came earlier in this surah: the polytheists' denial of the Messenger of God's mission, their description of the Qur'an as fabricated, their mockery of it and of what it brought concerning the Resurrection, beginning with His words ﴿When Our clear signs are recited to them, those who disbelieved say of the truth when it comes to them: "This is plain magic"﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 7], and what is connected with it, including the parable they were given of 'Ad. So He commanded the Messenger ﷺ to be patient with the harm he suffered from them, and gave him the example of the Messengers who were resolute.

It is also possible that the *fa'* is expressive (*fā' faṣīḥa*, a *fa'* that signals an implied condition). The sense would be: "When you have known what happened to the earlier nations, and known how We took vengeance on them and gave victory to Our Messengers, then be patient as they were patient."

*Ulu l-'Azm* means "the possessors of resolve," that is, those characterized by it.

*'Azm* (resolve) is a firm intention to act or speak without hesitation. God says: ﴿And when you have resolved, then put your trust in God﴾ [Al 'Imran: 159], and ﴿Do not determine upon the tie of marriage until the prescribed term reaches its end﴾ [al-Baqarah: 235]. Sa'd ibn Nashib, one of the poets of the *Hamasa*, said, meaning himself:

*When he resolves, he places his resolve before his eyes,
and turns aside from remembering the consequences.*

The praiseworthy resolve in religion is resolve upon what purifies the soul and secures the welfare of the community. Its foundation is patience in the face of what is disliked, its motive is piety (*taqwā*), and its strength is intense vigilance, such that the believer does not neglect to take account of himself. God says: ﴿But if you are patient and mindful of God, that is indeed of the steadfast matters﴾ [Al 'Imran: 186]. He also says: ﴿We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115]. This refers to the time before Adam descended into the world of obligation. On this view, *min* in His words *min al-rusul* ("from among the Messengers") is partitive (*tab'īḍiyya*). It is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "All the Messengers are *ulu l-'azm*," and on this view *min* is explicative (*bayāniyya*).

This verse implies that Muhammad ﷺ is among the *ulu l-'azm*, because likening the patience he was commanded to show to the patience of the resolute Messengers implies that he is their equal, since he complies with the command of his Lord. His patience is thus like theirs, and whoever is patient with their patience is, without doubt, one of them.

He follows the command to be patient with a prohibition against hastening [the punishment] for the polytheists, that is, against seeking its speedy arrival upon them: do not ask Us to bring it on them quickly. This is because hastening is incompatible with resolve, and because delaying the punishment lengthens the period of the Messenger's ﷺ patience, which strengthens his resolve.

The object of *tasta'jil* (seek to hasten) is omitted but implied by the context; its implied form is: "the punishment" or "the destruction."

The *lām* in *lahum* is the *lām* that transfers the action of hastening to an object for whose sake it is done, meaning: do not hasten for their sake. The sentence involves an omitted modifier, since the intended meaning is: do not hasten for their destruction.

The clause ﴿as if on the day they see what they are promised, they had not remained except for an hour of a day﴾ gives the reason for the prohibition against hastening the punishment for them, namely that the punishment will certainly befall them, so lengthening or hastening their term will have no effect on its occurrence. Murra ibn 'Adda al-Faq'asi said, and perhaps he took his saying from this verse:

*As if you were never given a night from time,
when you have reached what you were seeking.*

For them, at the arrival of the punishment, the long period of delay will resemble the absence of any respite except for a brief hour.

"*Min nahār*" ("of a day") describes the hour. It is specified with this description because an hour of daytime seems short to people, since they are occupied with many concerns during the day, whereas an hour of night seems long, since the one who stays awake finds nothing to occupy him. The indefiniteness (*tankīr*) here expresses paucity, as in the hadith about Friday in which the Prophet ﷺ said: "There is an hour in it in which supplication is answered," and he indicated with his hand that it is short. An hour is a part of time.

﴿This is a proclamation (*balāgh*)﴾. This is a summary (*fadhlaka*, a concluding recapitulation) of what came before, that it is a proclamation to mankind, believers and disbelievers alike, so that each may know his share of it. Thus His words *balāgh* ("a proclamation") are the predicate of an omitted subject, whose implied form is: "This is a proclamation," in the manner of a title or heading, like what is written at the top of an official document, "A decree from the Commander of the Faithful," or what is written at the top of deeds, such as "Deposit of a will," or what is written at the beginning of books, such as what appears in the *Muwatta'* (the *Wuqūt al-Salāh*, "Times of the Prayer"). Among this is what is written at the top of judicial and commercial announcements, the word *i'lān* ("announcement").

The demonstrative may appear, as in His words ﴿This is a proclamation to mankind﴾ [Ibrahim: 52], and in Sibawayh's saying: "This is a chapter on knowing what the words of Arabic are," and His words: ﴿Indeed in this is a proclamation for a people who worship﴾ [al-Anbiya': 106].

The sentence is a new independent sentence (*isti'nāf ibtidā'ī*), in the manner of a summary and conclusion, like the sentence ﴿That is ten complete﴾ and ﴿That is a community that has passed away﴾ [al-Baqarah: 134].

﴿Will any be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people?﴾ This is a consequence (*far'*) of the sentence ﴿as if on the day they see what they are promised﴾ down to "of a day": that is, the punishment will befall none except the polytheists like them.

The interrogative is used in the sense of negation, which is why an exception may follow it, as in His words ﴿And who would turn away from the religion of Abraham except one who makes a fool of himself?﴾ [al-Baqarah: 130].

The meaning of the consequence is that it has become clear from what you have heard that none will be destroyed except the defiantly disobedient people. This is from His words ﴿Say: I am not something new among the Messengers﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 9], and His words ﴿to warn those who have wronged, and as good news for the doers of good﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 12] down to His words ﴿nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 13], and His words ﴿And We have destroyed the towns around you﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 27], and so on.

"Destruction" (*ihlāk*) is used in both its literal and figurative senses. What was narrated earlier includes literal destruction, as in the story of 'Ad, and in His words ﴿And We have destroyed the towns around you﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 27]. Part of it is figurative, namely the evil state, that is, the punishment of the Hereafter. This applies to what was narrated concerning the punishment of the defiantly disobedient.

The definiteness of *al-qawm* ("the people") is generic (*ta'rīf al-jins*), which implies generality: all defiantly disobedient people. Thus it includes the polytheists of Mecca whom the Qur'an addresses, and so this consequence has the sense of a concluding remark (*tadhyīl*).

The use of the present tense in ﴿Will any be destroyed﴾ on this reading serves to give prominence (*taghlīb*) to the destruction of the polytheists, which has not yet occurred, over the destruction of the earlier nations.

You may also take the definiteness as definiteness by prior reference (*ta'rīf al-'ahd*), meaning the people spoken of in ﴿as if they, on the day they see what they are promised﴾ and what follows. In that case the explicit noun appears in place of a pronoun, to indicate the cause of their destruction, namely that it is polytheism.

The meaning of "defiant disobedience" (*fisq*) here is departure from faith, which is the defiant disobedience of polytheism.

The exception indicates that others will not perish in this destruction, or that they are those who believed and did righteous deeds.

In the name of God, the Most Merciful, the Especially Merciful.

Surah Muhammad. This surah is named in the books of Sunnah as "Surat Muhammad." It is also translated thus in the Sahih of al-Bukhari from the narration of Abu Dharr from al-Bukhari, and likewise in the exegetical works, where they say: "It is also called Surat al-Qital (The Surah of Fighting)."

In most narrations of the Sahih of al-Bukhari it appears as "Surat al-Ladhina Kafaru" (The Surah of Those Who Disbelieved).

The more famous name is the first, and its basis is that the Prophet's ﷺ name is mentioned in its second verse, so it became known by it before Surat Al 'Imran, in which is ﴿Muhammad is only a Messenger﴾ [Al 'Imran: 144].

As for naming it "Surat al-Anfal" (The Spoils of War), this is because the legislation of fighting is mentioned in it, and because the word itself is mentioned in it in His words ﴿and fighting is mentioned in it﴾ [Muhammad: 20]. Moreover, as will come, His words ﴿Those who believed say: "Why has a surah not been sent down?"﴾ [Muhammad: 20], down to ﴿and fighting is mentioned in it﴾ [Muhammad: 20], refer to this surah, so calling it "Surat al-Qital" is a naming found in the Qur'an itself.

It is Medinan by consensus, as reported by Ibn 'Atiyya and the author of *al-Itqan* (al-Suyuti). From al-Nasafi, however, it is reported that it is Meccan. al-Qurtubi reports from al-Tha'labi, al-Dahhak and Ibn Jubayr that it is Meccan. This is probably a mistake arising from what is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, that His words ﴿And how many a town was mightier in strength than your town﴾ [Muhammad: 13] were revealed on the road from Mecca before reaching Hira', that is, during the migration (*hijra*).

It is said that this surah was revealed after the day of Badr, and it is said that it was revealed concerning the battle of Uhud.

It is counted as the ninety-sixth in the order of the revelation of the surahs of the Qur'an. It was revealed after Surat al-Hadid and before Surat al-Ra'd.

Its verses were counted in most regions as thirty-nine. The people of Basra counted them as forty, and the people of Kufa as thirty-nine.

Its purposes:

Most of what is in this surah is an exhortation to fight the polytheists and an encouragement of the Muslims toward the reward of jihad.

It opens with what stirs the anger of the believers against the polytheists, because they disbelieved in God and barred [others] from His path, that is, His religion.

God informed the believers that He does not guide the polytheists in their deeds, and that He sets right the affairs of the believers. This was a guarantee to the believers of victory over their enemies.

It then moves on to the command to fight them and not to spare them.

It contains the promise of Paradise for those who strive, and the command to Muslims to struggle against the disbelievers and not to call them to peace, and a warning to the polytheists that they will suffer what befell the nations that denied before them.

It contains a description of Paradise and its bliss, and a description of Hell and its punishment.

It describes the hypocrites and their state of bewilderment when a surah is sent down containing the urging to fight, and their scant reflection on the Qur'an and their alliance with the polytheists.

It threatens the hypocrites that God will inform His Messenger ﷺ of their marks, and warns the Muslims not to let the hypocrisy of the hypocrites prevail over them.

It concludes with an allusion to the promise to the Muslims of the bestowal of authority, and warns them that if the affairs come to them, they must avoid corruption and severing of ties.
